(﴿And the example of the former peoples has passed on﴾ means: it has preceded in the verses, ﴿the example of the former peoples﴾.) ﴿We destroyed those who were mightier than them in strength﴾ means: in power, like the people of Hud, the people of Salih, and those similar to them. Allah destroyed them, and they were mightier than these who denied Muhammad (ﷺ), mightier in strength, and greater in wealth and children, yet all that did not avail them anything.

* In this verse: a demonstration of the great patience of the messengers, peace be upon them, for they were mocked while remaining patient until the command of Allah came. Otherwise, who could bear to call people while they mock him, were it not that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, strengthens a person with the firm word, as Allah said to His Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And had We not made you firm, you would almost have inclined toward them a little. Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life and double [punishment] in death﴾ [Al-Isra 74-75].

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning to Quraysh against rejecting the call of the Prophet (ﷺ), because Allah, the Exalted, threatened them by mentioning the destruction of those who came before. Every person has a heart; when he is told the condition of past nations and that they were destroyed, he must take heed, and he must fear and be mindful.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the permissibility of referring to something that came earlier, based on His saying: ﴿And the example of the former peoples has passed on﴾; i.e., their condition and attributes. Referral has a benefit, which is that a person remembers what has passed and returns to it.

Some people criticised the Hafiz Ibn Hajar (may Allah have mercy on him) for his frequent cross-references in Fath al-Bari, but in truth there is no fault in this. It is not an objection to this that he sometimes refers to something and we do not find what he referred to; sometimes he says, "It will come in the chapter on such-and-such," and you do not find it, because he may have been excused by forgetfulness, or he may have added it to a copy that did not reach us, or something similar.

The point is that the benefit of cross-references is reminding a person of what has preceded, and his attention to the book, and the wide circulation of the whole book; because if there are cross-references, it necessarily follows that you have the whole book, since it will be referred to, so you must have it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verse 9:

Then the Mighty and Majestic says: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Almighty, the All-Knowing."﴾ [az-Zukhruf 9].

﴿And if you asked them﴾: the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ). This sentence contains a condition and an oath. It contains a condition, which is (in) (if), and it contains an oath, indicated by the lam, because the lam is a preparatory lam (lam al-muwatta'ah) for the oath.

An oath requires a response, and a condition requires a response, does it not? The oath requires a response, which is the mention of what is sworn to, and the condition requires a response, which is the answer of the condition. When the two come together, which one do we place first? Ibn Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, says in his Alfiyyah:

"Omit, when a condition and an oath come together, the response of whichever comes last, and what is last is what is required to be omitted."

In the noble verse before us, which is the one that comes last: the oath or the condition?
* Students: The condition.

* The Shaykh: The condition. Therefore omit the response of the condition, and suffice with the response of the oath.

For this reason we find that the response in the verse is accompanied by the lam, which is ﴿layaqulunna﴾; and if this were the response of the condition, we would not have needed the lam.

﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say﴾: the nun of the nominative has been dropped from it, because of the succession of nuns, and the wa of the pronoun, because of the meeting of two sukun letters: ﴿layaqulunna﴾. Its original form before the deletion was: layaqulūnanna. How many nuns do we have here? Three. Drop the first, because its deletion is common; that is, the deletion of the nun of the nominative from the imperfect is frequent, and because the nun of emphasis came for a purpose, and if we deleted it the purpose, which is emphasis, would be lost. So we drop the nun of the nominative, which is the first nun, because of the succession of nuns.

Then comes the turn of the pronoun (layaqulūnanna). Why did we drop the wāw? We dropped it because of the meeting of two sukūn letters: the two sukūn letters are the wāw, which is quiescent, and the first of the doubled nuns, which is quiescent, so the wāw is dropped. This explanation is undoubtedly that of the grammarians; for otherwise, when an Arab speaks these words, does it occur to his mind that he dropped the nun of the nominative and then dropped the wāw of the pronoun, and so on? No, but the scholars of grammar, may Allah have mercy on them, seek explanations for the speech of the Arabs, and they found this explanation.

If you were to say to them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would say, ﴿They were created by the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾ [az-Zukhruf 9]. Look at the answer; it is a completely correct answer.

﴿Khalaqahunna﴾ means: the heavens and the earth. ﴿al-'Azīz﴾ means the One possessing 'izzah, and the most prominent meaning of 'izzah is domination (al-ghalabah). It is said: "So-and-so became mighty ('azza), and so he prevailed." It has another meaning, which is qadr, that is, nobility and exaltation, and a third meaning, which is strength and firmness, from which comes their saying: "a hard (ʿazāz) land," meaning firm and solid.

If we wish to apply these meanings to the attribute of might with which Allah has described Himself, we say: He is ʿAzīz from ʿizz, which is domination; ʿAzīz from the 'izzat al-qadr (the might of dignity), and it is well known that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is greater in dignity than everything.

The third: the 'izzah of firmness, strength and inaccessibility, because Allah, the Exalted, is far removed from being described with any evil or any defect.

﴿al-ʿAlīm﴾ means the One possessing complete knowledge. Reflect on how they brought this phrase, ﴿al-ʿAzīz al-ʿAlīm﴾, as an indication that they acknowledge they are humble before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and that everything in the heavens and the earth proceeds from knowledge ﴿al-ʿAzīz al-ʿAlīm﴾. This acknowledgement necessarily requires that they acknowledge there is no god but Allah, but they did not do so.

* From this noble verse: evidence that the polytheists acknowledge Tawhid al-Rububiyyah (the oneness of Lordship), by their saying in reply: ﴿They were created by the Almighty, the All-Knowing﴾, and the matter is as they said. Their acknowledgement of Tawhid al-Rububiyyah obliges them to acknowledge Tawhid al-Uluhiyyah (the oneness of worship). It is said to them: if you acknowledge that there is no creator except Allah, then acknowledge that there is no true object of worship except Allah.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: that the heavens are numbered, by His saying ﴿as-samawāt﴾, and it has come in the Noble Qur'an and in the Prophetic Sunnah that the number of the heavens is seven. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿It is Allah who created seven heavens﴾ [at-Talaq 12].

As for the earth, there is no explicit statement in the Qur'an that it is seven, but the apparent meaning of the Qur'an is so, such as His saying: ﴿It is Allah who created seven heavens and of the earth the like of them﴾ [at-Talaq 12]. The likeness here cannot be in size or in strength, because the heavens are wider, greater and stronger than the earth, so nothing remains except number.

The Sunnah has also come explicitly on this. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever takes unjustly a span of land, it will be hung around his neck from seven earths on the Day of Resurrection."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3198) and Muslim, and the wording is his (1610), from the hadith of Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl (may Allah be pleased with him), and its wording is: "Whoever takes unjustly a span of land, Allah will hang it around his neck from seven earths on the Day of Resurrection."]]

The heavens are layered (ṭibāq), one above the other, and if one is above the other, it follows that the second heaven is wider than the first, does it not? Yes, because it encircles it; the third is wider than the second, and so on. For this reason the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And the heaven We built with might, and indeed We are expanding it﴾ [adh-Dhariyat 47]. The higher one ascends through the heavens, the wider the heavens become. They are layers without doubt, as in the Noble Qur'an, and as is stated explicitly in the hadith of the Mi'raj.

As for the earth, it too is layered, as evidenced by the fact that whoever takes a span of the earth on which we live, it is hung around him from seven earths. Were it not that the second earth is beneath, and the third beneath it, and so on, a person would not be hung with seven earths, for he only seized the surface of the earth; so the earths are layered.

As for how these layers are, we have not yet arrived at knowledge of them, and geologists who dig into the depths of the earth do not reach this; it is unknown to us. But the hadith, "it will be hung around his neck from seven earths on the Day of Resurrection," indicates what?

* Student: That they are layers.

* The Shaykh: That they are layers.

* From the benefits of this verse: the affirmation of these two names of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿al-ʿAzīz al-ʿAlīm﴾.

Know, my brother, that every name of Allah includes an attribute: al-ʿAzīz includes the attribute of ʿizzah, and al-ʿAlīm includes the attribute of knowledge. Not every attribute from which a name is derived is itself a name; therefore we say that the domain of attributes is wider than the domain of names, because there are attributes for which Allah has no name, but there is no name without an attribute derived from it. And Allah knows best.

* Student: (...) is his repentance accepted?

* The Shaykh: The correct view is that it is accepted if he establishes evidence that he is sincere. But if he is toying with us, saying he has repented while remaining as he is, we do not accept it.

* Student: Is he killed?

* The Shaykh: He is killed, yes, by killing him, as long as we do not know that he has repented.

* Student: May Allah reward you with good, O Shaykh. We mentioned that for these shirk acts by Muslims we do not judge them as polytheists until proof is established against them; the same applies to those who commit innovations?

* The Shaykh: Yes indeed, but the innovator is more severe, because the innovator, may Allah protect us, leads many people astray through himself.

* Student: Shirk?

* The Shaykh: It harms only its doer, except that if this polytheist has obedience among his people, (...) a leader among his people whom they follow (...). But if he is a commoner, it affects only himself. For this reason some scholars said: the innovator has no repentance, because even if he repents himself, he is not safe from the misguidance of those who followed him.

* Student: May Allah be good to you. What is the meaning of His saying, ﴿until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾ [al-A'raf 40]?

* The Shaykh: The meaning is that this is a suspension on something impossible: ﴿The gates of heaven will not be opened for them, nor will they enter Paradise until the camel passes through the eye of the needle﴾. The camel is the well-known animal. As for the view of some who say it is a thick rope, this is a false view, because Allah did not say "until the camel is made to enter"; He said "until the camel enters." Does a rope have a will to enter and exit? Answer me.

* Student: No.

* The Shaykh: What is it that enters and exits?

* Student: The camel; the beast.

* The Shaykh: The camel, the animal. So the correct view is that what is meant is the real camel, and the meaning is that it is impossible for them to enter Paradise, just as it is impossible for a camel to enter the eye of a needle, the hole of the needle. This is like the saying of the poet:

"When the crow turns white, I will come to my family, and tar becomes like milk, fresh and white."
Is this possible? The crow cannot become white, and tar cannot be like milk.

* Student: May Allah be good to you. If a polytheist was approached by a Muslim who is a Sufi, and Islam reached him in the manner of Sufism and the traces of innovators, so he began to act on this and believe that this is Islam, will he be held accountable for it?

* The Shaykh: No. (...) comes from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, not from anyone else. No one can be punished for falsehood unless he knows it is falsehood. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is more merciful and wiser than to punish a person who does not know. But there are obstinate people to whom the truth is mentioned and who say: "No, I want to follow my shaykh." Even if the one who mentioned the truth is a well-known scholar, he says: "No, I want to follow my shaykhs." Such a person is not excused. But if a commoner informs him: "O Allah, this act is not permissible, this is shirk," while all his shaykhs say: "This is good," is such a person excused or not excused?

* Student: Not excused if he knows the truth.

* Another student: Excused.

* The Shaykh: He did not know the truth; he has shaykhs whom he regards as truly shaykhs. If a commoner in the market came and said: "This is shirk," is he excused or not?

* Student: He is excused.

* The Shaykh: He is excused, because he does not trust it; the truth did not reach him in a way that he could trust. Now, as for our scholars: if someone came to us contrary to what our scholars say, and we do not know him, we would not follow him. But it may be said that being informed that he is upon falsehood and that the truth is the opposite obliges him to search and ask, so he may be held accountable on this basis, namely for negligence in seeking the truth.

* Student: O Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, some Sufis give litanies (adhkar) to their disciples on condition that if they neglect something, they become disbelievers?

* The Shaykh: This is a problem. And these are the common Muslims?

* Student: Yes, they say: "If we leave something, we become disbelievers."

* The Shaykh: No. Moreover, these people are deceived by the outward appearance of the Sufi. The outward state of the Sufi is that he is pious; you find him always in humility, and perhaps you find him weeping, then he brings the litanies in a manner that excites a person. This is a trial, and we seek refuge in Allah.

* Student: O Shaykh, may Allah preserve you, what is the ruling on one who mocks the people of religion?

* The Shaykh: The one who mocks the people of religion: if he mocks them for their religion, then he is mocking religion; but if he mocks them for their appearance, then no. For this reason, if they found anyone who lifted his garment to mid-calf among the reputable and obeyed scholars, you would not find anyone mocking them; but if a common ordinary person came, they would mock him. Here we say: mockery is not mockery of religion, but mockery of this man, and it is obligatory to distinguish between this and that.

* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Almighty, the All-Knowing." (9) He who made for you the earth as a cradle and made for you therein roads that you may be guided. (10) And He who sends down from the sky water in measure, and We revive therewith a dead land. Thus you will be brought forth﴾ [az-Zukhruf 9-11].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And how many a prophet We sent among the former peoples﴾ [az-Zukhruf 6]. What is this ﴿kam﴾?

* Student: Multiplicative (takthiriyyah).

* The Shaykh: Multiplicative, and it is called?

* Student: For number.

* Another student: It is called khabariyyah (informative).

* The Shaykh: It is called khabariyyah. So what is the meaning of ﴿kam ahlaknā﴾?

* Student: How much We destroyed.

* The Shaykh: Yes; that is, We destroyed many before you, and We sent many prophets.

Did every nation have a messenger sent to it?

* Student: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes. What is the evidence?

* Student: ﴿And We had already sent messengers before you﴾ [ar-Ra'd 38].

* The Shaykh: No.

* Student: ﴿And there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them﴾ [Fatir 24].

* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿And there was no nation but that a warner had passed among them﴾, and reason requires this; that is, transmitted evidence and rational evidence.

Good. What was the condition of the former nations with regard to the messengers?

* Student: They mocked them.

* The Shaykh: Mockery of them. The evidence?

* Student: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And there never came to them a messenger but that they mocked him﴾ [al-Hijr 11].

* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿And there never came to them a messenger but that they mocked him﴾.

Good. ﴿We destroyed those who were greater than them﴾: to whom does the pronoun refer?

* Student: ﴿We destroyed those who were greater than them﴾: Quraysh.

* The Shaykh: Quraysh. Well done. And what is the meaning of ﴿baṭshan﴾?

* Student: Strength.

* The Shaykh: Strength. An example of that?

* Student: ʿĀd.

* The Shaykh: ʿĀd, for they were among the strongest of people, to the extent that they said: ﴿Who is stronger than us in strength?﴾ [Fussilat 15], so Allah destroyed them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verse 10–11:

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And if you asked them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing." (9) He who made for you the earth a cradle and made for you therein roads [ṭuruqan, paths] ﴿so that you may be guided﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 9, 10].

His saying: ﴿He who made for you﴾ is not part of the speech of those whom the Prophet ﷺ asked. Their speech ends at His saying: ﴿"They were created by the All-Mighty, the All-Knowing."﴾ As for ﴿He who made for you the earth a cradle﴾, this is the speech of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The meaning of ﴿ja'ala﴾ (made, rendered) is ṣayyara (made into). ﴿For you the earth a cradle﴾ means: like a cradle, smoothed out, a resting place in which a person finds tranquility.

﴿And made for you therein roads﴾ means: He made for you therein roads (subul), i.e., paths (ṭuruq). These paths lie between the ravines, the mountains and the lowlands, so that even strong winds come, yet these paths remain known. The paths are sought out by means of the mountains, the ravines and the stars, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿and landmarks; and by the star they are guided﴾ [An-Nahl 16].

﴿And made for you therein roads so that you may be guided﴾: (la'alla, "so that") here denotes causation (ta'līl). It is well known that la'alla comes for causation, as here, and comes for hope (tarajjī), and comes for expectation (tawaqquʿ). What determines the meaning is the context of the speech and the indications of the circumstances.

﴿So that you may be guided﴾ follows, the explanation:

* A student: (To your destinations in your journeys).

* The Shaykh: Yes, ﴿so that you may be guided﴾ means: that you may know the routes. So the guidance here is guidance to routes. (To your destinations in your journeys.) Now, praise be to Allah, paved and clear roads have come into existence between cities, villages and other places, all of this by the blessing of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. I think you have ﴿He who made for you the earth a cradle﴾.

* A student: (...).

* The Shaykh: I have here ﴿﴿mihādan﴾﴾, and he did not point to the reading that is in the Mushaf. It is in two readings: ﴿﴿mihādan﴾﴾, and it has come in another verse with this wording, and ﴿mahdan﴾, which means mihād.

﴿And He who sent down from the sky water in measure, and We revived thereby a dead land﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 11]. ﴿He who sent down from the sky water﴾ means: He sent it down little by little. You find the rain descending from the sky in drops, and if it came like the mouths of waterskins, it would ruin the earth and demolish buildings. But by the mercy of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, He made it descend little by little; yet despite that, the valleys flow with it even though it falls drop by drop. But with its abundance, the ravines flow with it.

﴿He who sent down from the sky water﴾: "the sky" here is meant as height. Know that "sky" (samā') is used with two meanings. The first meaning: height in itself. The second meaning: the protected ceiling, which is the seven heavens.

So His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth﴾ [Al-Baqarah 164], the sky here means the protected ceiling; likewise His saying: ﴿And We made the sky a protected ceiling﴾ [Al-Anbiya' 32].

As for His saying: ﴿sent down from the sky﴾, what is meant is height, because rain does not descend from the sky itself, but descends from the height, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth﴾. The cloud is not clinging to the sky; rather it is between the sky and the earth, and it is nearer to the earth.

(﴿sent down from the sky water in measure﴾ means: in the measure of your need for it, and He did not send it down as a flood.) His saying: ﴿in measure﴾, the author explained it as: in the measure of what you need. It has another meaning: ﴿in measure﴾, meaning it is determined and specified; even the drop, Allah has known it, and known how it descends, when it descends, and where it descends. Everything is by measure. Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, all things We created with measure﴾ [Al-Qamar 49]. So the meaning according to this is that this rain, despite its abundance and the number of its drops, descends in a specified measure. The meaning the author mentioned is a correct meaning, and the verse admits of this and that. Our rule in tafsir is: when a word in the Qur'an or the Sunnah admits of two meanings equally, with no contradiction between them, it must be understood as both, for the broadening of meaning.

﴿and We revived thereby a dead land﴾: ﴿ansharnā﴾ means: We gave life, as is shown in other verses, in His saying: ﴿And He who sent down from the sky water in measure, and We revived thereby a dead land﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 11]. So ﴿ansharnā﴾ means: We gave life. This is something observed: you find the earth barren and withered, with no greenery in it, and when the rain descends, it becomes stirring with vegetation of every lovely pair.

His saying: (We gave life ﴿thereby to a dead land. Thus﴾ means: like this giving of life, ﴿you will be brought forth﴾) means: just as We gave life to the earth by rain, likewise We will give you life on the Day of Resurrection. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said in another verse: ﴿And among His signs is that you see the earth humbled﴾, lifeless, ﴿but when We send down upon it water, it stirs and swells﴾, meaning it rises with its plants, ﴿Indeed, He who gave it life is the Giver of life to the dead; indeed He is over all things Competent﴾ [Fussilat 39].

* In these verses there are benefits:

* Among them: the demonstration of Allah's blessing, Mighty and Majestic, in that He made the earth a cradle for us. Had it been hard, we would not have settled upon it, tilled it, or benefited from it much; had it been loose in the same way, we would not have benefited from it and our feet would have sunk into it. But from Allah's blessing is that He made it like a cradle.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: Allah's blessing upon us in the roads He made for us on this earth across its distant regions. But by what do we find the roads? We mentioned that they are sought by the ravines, the mountains, and likewise the stars.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: the affirmation of Allah's wisdom in what He creates, in His saying: ﴿so that you may be guided﴾. Allah's wisdom, Mighty and Majestic, in what He creates and in what He legislates is established; but among wisdoms are some we know, and among them are some we do not know because of the shortness of our understanding, and among wisdoms are some that many people know and that remain hidden from many others.

* Among the benefits of the noble verse: an indication that if the sensory goal requires roads, then so does the intangible goal, which is reaching the abode of Allah's honor, Mighty and Majestic. It requires roads; we must travel these roads until we reach the goal, and if we do not travel them, we will not reach the goal.

* Among the benefits of the second verse: Allah's power, Mighty and Majestic, in sending down rain.

* Among them: Allah's mercy, Mighty and Majestic, in sending down rain from above; for had it come from below, the lower earth would have been drowned without the water reaching the mountain peaks. But Allah, Exalted is He, made it descend from above so that it waters the high and the low; and when the high is watered, it descends to the low.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that this water descending from the sky descends in measure, in both of the meanings we mentioned.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that Allah, Exalted is He, gives life to the earth after its death by this water.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the application of the word "death" to what has no soul; that is, what has no soul that perceives, given His saying: ﴿a dead land﴾. Otherwise, it is well known that the earth does not have the life of animals, the life of sensation, but rather the life of growth.

* Among the benefits of the verse: analogy of the intelligible upon the sensible, or if you wish, analogy of the absent upon the present, given His saying: ﴿Thus you will be brought forth﴾.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of analogy (qiyās) and that it is a proof. But is it a rational proof or a textual proof?

The answer: it is a rational proof, established by textual proof; because the mind moves from the analogue (maqīs ʿalayh) to the analogized (maqīs), so it is rational in terms of the manner of reasoning from it, and textual in terms of its being legislatively established.

* Among the benefits of the second verse: Allah's power, Mighty and Majestic, in sending down rain.

* Among them: Allah's mercy, Mighty and Majestic, in sending down rain from above; for had it come from below, the lower earth would have been drowned without the water reaching the mountain peaks. But Allah, Exalted is He, made it descend from above so that it waters the high and the low; and when the high is watered, it descends to the low.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that this water descending from the sky descends in measure, in both of the meanings we mentioned.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that Allah, Exalted is He, gives life to the earth after its death by this water.

* Among the benefits of the verse: the application of the word "death" to what has no soul; that is, what has no soul that perceives, given His saying: ﴿a dead land﴾. Otherwise, it is well known that the earth does not have the life of animals, the life of sensation, but rather the life of growth.

* Among the benefits of the verse: analogy of the intelligible upon the sensible, or if you wish, analogy of the absent upon the present, given His saying: ﴿Thus you will be brought forth﴾.

* Among its benefits: the affirmation of analogy (qiyās) and that it is a proof. But is it a rational proof or a textual proof?

The answer: it is a rational proof, established by textual proof; because the mind moves from the analogue (maqīs ʿalayh) to the analogized (maqīs), so it is rational in terms of the manner of reasoning from it, and textual in terms of its being legislatively established.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verse 12–14:

﴿And He who created all the pairs﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 12]. This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with what came before, and it is of the type of conjoining attributes (ʿaṭf al-ṣifat), not of the type of conjoining essences (ʿaṭf al-dhawat). The basic rule in conjunction (ʿaṭf) is that it be between two things different in their essence. This is the principle. But when evidence establishes that the essence is one, it becomes conjunction of attributes.

Consider the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who created and proportioned, and who determined and guided, and who brought forth the pasture﴾ [Al-A'la: 1–4]. This conjunction is of the type of conjoining attributes, because the one described is one. But the basic rule in conjunction is that it is of the type of what? The difference of essences, unless evidence establishes that the conjoined and the conjoined-to are one thing, in which case it is the conjoining of attributes, some of them with others, for one described.

The verses we have before us: which of the two types are they? They are of the type of conjoining attributes, because the one described is one.

﴿And He who created all the pairs﴾. "Al-azwaj" (the pairs) here means the kinds (aṣnaf), as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Gather those who did wrong and their pairs﴾ [As-Saffat: 22], meaning their kinds. And He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿And other [punishments] of similar kind, in pairs﴾ [Sad: 58].

﴿Created all the pairs﴾, that is, the kinds, all the kinds. The one who created them is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. You are amazed when you come to a garden and find these trees, some of whose flowers are red, some blue, some yellow, colored. Who created them and colored them? It is Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

The verse may also carry another meaning: ﴿created all the pairs﴾, meaning the two paired things from which a third is produced, such as male and female, negative and positive, and what is similar to that. The verse admits both meanings together, and they are not contradictory, so it is understood as both.

(﴿Created all the pairs, and made for you of the ships﴾, the ships, ﴿and the livestock﴾ such as camels, ﴿that you ride﴾.) ﴿Made for you﴾ means "appointed." His saying ﴿that you ride﴾ is the object of ﴿made﴾, that is, ﴿made for you of the ships﴾, which are the sea ships, and people did not know anything else before. Now there have come the air ships, and they are what?

* A student: The airplanes.

* The Shaykh: The airplanes. As for the livestock, such as camels, mules and others that are ridden.

﴿He made for you of the ships and the livestock that which you ride﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 12], that is, that which you ride. This is one of the blessings of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿So that you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾. The lam here is the lam of consequence (lām al-ʿāqibah), not the lam of causation, because it is possible for a person to have many livestock, many camels, and not ride them. But the lam is for consequence.

The lam of consequence occurs often in the Qur'an and elsewhere, and among its examples is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ [Al-Qasas: 8]. The lam in His saying ﴿that he might become﴾ is not the lam of causation, because the family of Pharaoh did not pick him up for this purpose; rather they picked him up and this outcome resulted. Such a lam is called the lam of consequence.

As for His saying ﴿so that you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾, that is, that you may mount upon them and settle upon them. ﴿Upon their backs﴾ (he says: he made the pronoun singular and the back plural, considering the wording of "mā" and its meaning).

﴿So that you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾: he made "backs" plural and did not say "upon its back", and he made the pronoun singular and did not say "upon their backs", considering the wording of "mā" and its meaning. This is because "mā" is suitable for the singular and the plural. Sometimes its wording is observed, and sometimes its meaning. When the wording is observed, the pronoun is made singular; when the meaning is observed, it follows the intended meaning. Likewise "man" (who) is sometimes treated according to its wording and sometimes according to its meaning. Read the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness, He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever﴾ [At-Talaq: 11]. In ﴿And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness, He will admit him﴾ he observed what?

* Students: The wording.

* The Shaykh: The wording; he made it singular, ﴿abiding therein﴾ is the meaning.

﴿So that you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾, that is, the backs of what you ride of the ships and the livestock. He made them plural in view of meaning, and singular in view of wording.

﴿So that you may sit firmly upon their backs, then remember the blessing of your Lord when you are settled upon them﴾. For if a person settles upon the ship or upon the livestock, he remembers the blessing of Allah upon him, since He made this mount easy for him. Had Allah not made it easy, he would not have been able to do this. Had Allah made camels difficult, they could not be ridden, and people would not have benefited from them. Had ships been lacking, people could not have crossed from dry land to dry land. So let a person remember the blessing of Allah when he is settled upon its back. ﴿And say﴾, that is, with your tongues, acknowledging with your hearts: ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us﴾, that is, made it submissive to us; ﴿and we could not have it [by our own strength]﴾, that is, capable of it (﴿muqrinīn﴾: able). ﴿And indeed, to our Lord we will return﴾; he said: (returning).

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the blessing of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, upon His servants, in that He made for them of ships and livestock what they ride. We have mentioned that the ship (fulk) includes the air ship and the sea ship, and we may say also the land ship, such as motor vehicles; these are ships too. So ships are aerial, marine and land.

* Among the benefits of this verse: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, subjected the livestock to us, in that He made them subservient for us to ride and carry, while they are submissive before us; this is from His saying: ﴿And made for you of the ships and the livestock﴾.

* Among the benefits of this verse: it is fitting for a person, when he rides livestock and likewise ships, to make his mount comfortable; this is from His saying: ﴿So that you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾, since if it were not comfortable, the blessing would not be complete. So he should make it comfortable as far as possible and according to circumstances.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: it is fitting for a person to remember the blessing of Allah upon him in what He has subjected for him of ships and livestock; this is from His saying: ﴿then remember the blessing of your Lord﴾. The word "blessing" here is singular with a genitive attached, so is the intent to mention all blessings or the blessing suited to the situation? The apparent meaning is the second, because a person, when riding, may not call to mind all blessings, such as wealth, children, security and tranquillity, but he remembers the blessing present.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the recommendation of this remembrance when mounting, which is: ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it [by our own strength]. And indeed, to our Lord we will return.﴾

If someone says: why was the word "Glory be" (subḥān) chosen rather than, for example, "Allah is greatest"?

The answer: glorifying Allah (tasbīḥ) means declaring Him free of every deficiency and defect. The human being, by contrast, is in need of riding, so he is deficient; it was fitting that he say: ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us﴾, so that he remembers thereby that he himself is in need of these mounts, and that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is exalted above need.

That is, if someone says: why did he not say "How great is Allah's favour upon you" or "Allah is greatest"?

The answer: when he saw himself in need of riding, he declared Allah, Mighty and Majestic, free of need, and said: ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that we remember Allah's blessing upon us in subjecting these livestock; this is from His saying: ﴿Who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it [by our own strength]﴾; that is, capable of it. Had Allah not subjected the camel to us, we could not have managed it. The camel is stronger than us and bigger than us in body. If Allah, glorified and exalted, had made it difficult, could anyone settle upon it, or load it, or take it into any place he wished, or take it out whenever he wished? No, but Allah subjected it to us.

* Among the noble benefits of the verse: the servant's acknowledgment of his own weakness and frailty; this is from His saying: ﴿and we could not have it [by our own strength]﴾; that is, capable of it.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that when a person rides these mounts he remembers the final riding, which is the goal of the world; this is from His saying: ﴿And indeed, to our Lord we will return﴾. The author's explanation of it, may God have mercy on him, as "departing" (al-inṣirāf), that is, "we are turning back to Allah", is deficient; the correct view is what we have mentioned: that when you ride, remember your riding upon the bier when you are turned over to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. In this there is a reminder of a future state for the children of Adam, which is the state of being turned back to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Is this remembrance specific to when one rides for travel, or is it general?

The answer: it is general. Whenever you ride a car, a camel or an airplane, remember this: ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it [by our own strength]. And indeed, to our Lord we will return.﴾

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the recommendation of this remembrance when mounting, which is: ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it [by our own strength]. And indeed, to our Lord we will return.﴾

If someone says: why was the word "Glory be" (subḥān) chosen rather than, for example, "Allah is greatest"?

The answer: glorifying Allah (tasbīḥ) means declaring Him free of every deficiency and defect. The human being, by contrast, is in need of riding, so he is deficient; it was fitting that he say: ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us﴾, so that he remembers thereby that he himself is in need of these mounts, and that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is exalted above need.

That is, if someone says: why did he not say "How great is Allah's favour upon you" or "Allah is greatest"?

The answer: when he saw himself in need of riding, he declared Allah, Mighty and Majestic, free of need, and said: ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us﴾.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that we remember Allah's blessing upon us in subjecting these livestock; this is from His saying: ﴿Who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it [by our own strength]﴾; that is, capable of it. Had Allah not subjected the camel to us, we could not have managed it. The camel is stronger than us and bigger than us in body. If Allah, glorified and exalted, had made it difficult, could anyone settle upon it, or load it, or take it into any place he wished, or take it out whenever he wished? No, but Allah subjected it to us.

* Among the noble benefits of the verse: the servant's acknowledgment of his own weakness and frailty; this is from His saying: ﴿and we could not have it [by our own strength]﴾; that is, capable of it.

* Among the benefits of the verse: that when a person rides these mounts he remembers the final riding, which is the goal of the world; this is from His saying: ﴿And indeed, to our Lord we will return﴾. The author's explanation of it, may God have mercy on him, as "departing" (al-inṣirāf), that is, "we are turning back to Allah", is deficient; the correct view is what we have mentioned: that when you ride, remember your riding upon the bier when you are turned over to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. In this there is a reminder of a future state for the children of Adam, which is the state of being turned back to Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Is this remembrance specific to when one rides for travel, or is it general?

The answer: it is general. Whenever you ride a car, a camel or an airplane, remember this: ﴿Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us, and we could not have it [by our own strength]. And indeed, to our Lord we will return.﴾

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verse 15–16 (part 1 of 2):

Then Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a part. Indeed, mankind is clearly ungrateful.﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 15]. ﴿And they have made﴾: the pronoun refers to the polytheists of Quraysh; i.e., they designated. ﴿for Him﴾: i.e., for Allah. ﴿from His servants﴾: i.e., from His creatures, and all creatures are servants of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; and what is meant by "servants" here is the angels. ﴿a part﴾: i.e., a portion of Him; since they said: the angels are the daughters of Allah; the Jews said: 'Uzayr is the son of Allah; the Christians said: the Messiah is the son of Allah.
As for His saying ﴿a part﴾: because the child is a part of his father, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said about his daughter Fatimah: "She is a piece of my flesh."[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (3714) and Muslim (2449/94) with their chain from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Fatimah is a piece of me; whoever angers her angers me."]]
These polytheists, may Allah protect us, have made for Allah from His servants a part. And reflect on His saying ﴿from His servants﴾: it becomes clear to you that their being servants of Allah utterly precludes that they be a part of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; for the worshipped is not the worshipper, so it is impossible for the worshipper to be a part of the worshipped.
﴿Indeed, mankind is clearly ungrateful﴾: what is meant is the genus; i.e., indeed the genus of mankind is manifestly ungrateful to a clear degree. It is not objected to this that some of mankind are fully faithful believers; for we say: it may be intended as a genus, as in His saying: ﴿And mankind bore it; indeed, he was a wrongdoer, ignorant﴾ [Al-Ahzab 72], and the believer is not a wrongdoer or ignorant, but the genus of mankind is wrongdoing and ignorant.
If someone says: do we interpret every such expression as referring to the genus?
The answer: No. We do not interpret it as the genus unless evidence establishes this; otherwise the default is generality, as in His saying: ﴿And mankind was created weak﴾ [An-Nisa 28]. Is this meant as the genus or every individual? It means every individual. But when it is impossible to interpret it as generality, we make it the genus.
Let me give you an example to clarify the matter: "The man is better than the woman." What is meant is the genus, and the meaning is not that every one of the men is better than every woman; for among women are those who are better than many men. Rather, what is meant is the genus; i.e., this genus is better than that genus.
* Student: May Allah bless you, Shaykh. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, began this surah with His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾...
The genus; we make it the genus.
And let me give you an example to clarify the matter: "The man is better than the woman." What is meant?
* Students: The genus.
* Shaykh: The genus, and the meaning is not that every one of the men is better than every woman; for among women are those who are better than many men. Rather, what is meant is the genus; i.e., this genus is better than that genus.
* Student: May Allah bless you, Shaykh. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, began this surah with His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 3], then He said: ﴿Who made for you the earth a cradle﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 10], then He said, Glorified and Exalted is He: ﴿And made for you of the ships﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 12]; made, made, made, then came after it: ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a part﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 15]. Is there a connection between them..?
* Shaykh: Harmony.
* Student: Harmony, yes.
* Shaykh: It may be said that this is verbal harmony, since sometimes speech is more eloquent when it follows a single pattern, so this falls under verbal harmony.
* Student: The supplication upon arriving at a place: "I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah"[[Recorded by Muslim (2708/54) from the hadith of Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, may Allah be pleased with him.]]. Is it specific to travel or general?
* Shaykh: No, it is general; even if you alight in a place, you say: "I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah," and at sleep you say: "I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah," and at the edges of night and day: "I seek refuge in the perfect words of Allah."
* Student: The mosque?
* Shaykh: The mosque has a specific remembrance, and a mosque is not a place where a person alights; rather he stays there for a specific act of obedience and then walks away.
* Student: May Allah preserve you, Shaykh; is this supplication "Glory be to Him who subjected this to us" legislated for the electric elevator?
* Shaykh: This is open to consideration; for this electric elevator is like a staircase and not like a mount that travels. It ascends upward, so considering it among the means of conveyance is questionable.
* Student: The explanation of ﴿We have made it﴾?
* Shaykh: It means: We rendered it. Sometimes (ja'ala) means ṣayyara (to render), and sometimes means khalaqa (to create), according to context; if it governs two objects it means ṣayyara, and if it governs one object it means khalaqa, like the Most High's saying: ﴿And He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [Al-An'am 1]; this is in the sense of khalaqa, because it governs only one object. But if it governs two objects, it means ṣayyara.
* Student: Shaykh, His saying: ﴿So that you may be guided﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 10]; the intended guidance is the guidance of the roads, as you mentioned, Your Eminence. Can it be interpreted as the guidance of taking lesson from the verse?
* Shaykh: No; the basis of this prevents it.
* Student: Shaykh, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾, there are some words in the Qur'an whose origin is foreign (...)?
* Shaykh: This one asks: despite ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾, there are some words in the Qur'an whose origin is not Arabic. We say: when the Arabs spoke them they became Arabic through usage, even if their origin is not Arabic.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a part. Indeed, mankind is clearly ungrateful (15). Or has He taken from what He creates daughters and chosen you for sons? (16) And when one of them is given good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful, his face becomes darkened, and he suppresses grief (17). Is one who is brought up in ornaments and is in dispute not clear? (18). And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 15–19].
* Shaykh: All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah send blessings and peace upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family, companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.
To proceed: the interpretation of the Great Qur'an is among the most important duties of Muslims, that they understand the meaning of the speech of Allah, Glorified and Exalted; for speech whose meaning is not understood is not benefited from, and one who reads without understanding is like the unlettered who does not read, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And among them are unlettered ones who do not know the Book except wishful thinking﴾ [Al-Baqarah 78]; i.e., except recitation, so Allah named them unlettered.
The Qur'an is explained by the Qur'an; if not, then by the Sunnah; if not, then by the sayings of the Companions, especially those well known for knowledge of tafsir; if not, then by what the senior Successors among the people of tafsir said. This is the principle followed by the People of the Sunnah and the Community.
As for interpretation by opinion (ra'y), some who do it are mistaken and some are correct, but it is not permissible for a person to interpret the Qur'an by his opinion, meaning to bend the Qur'an to his opinion; for whoever speaks about the Qur'an by his opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire.
An example of that: those who interpret the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 64] as meaning bounty. These have spoken about the Qur'an by their opinion, because this meaning is definitely not what is intended. Likewise those who say ﴿He istawa over the Throne﴾ [Al-A'raf 54] means He seized control of the Throne; this is a reprehensible statement, and interpreting the verse thus is speaking about Allah without knowledge, a fabrication against Allah, Glorified and Exalted.
We say of these that they spoke about the Qur'an by their opinion; i.e., they bent the Qur'an to their opinion. As for one who interprets the Qur'an according to the established legal and linguistic realities, when there is no legal technical meaning, he has not spoken about the Qur'an by his opinion.
This principle was already mentioned when we first began the science of tafsir, so let it be a reference for you. Is the Qur'an interpreted first by...?
* Students: By the Qur'an.
* Shaykh: Then?
* Students: By the Sunnah.
* Shaykh: Then?
* Students: By the sayings of the Companions.
* Shaykh: Then?
* Students: The senior Successors.
* Shaykh: The senior Successors who gave attention to tafsir, such as Mujahid ibn Jabr, may Allah have mercy on him, who took tafsir from Abdullah ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.
We previously noted in tafsir that Allah, Most High, analogized the unseen to the seen. What is that?
* Student: His saying, Most High: ﴿Thus you will be brought forth﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 11].
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: He analogized the seen, which is the giving of life...
* Shaykh: No, what is the seen? He analogized the unseen, which is the reviving of the dead, to the seen that they witness: He sent down water from the sky and with it brought forth every fruit. So He analogized the future to the present, and this is one of the methods of teaching and making understood.
His saying: ﴿Water from the sky﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 11]; what is meant by "sky"?
* Student: The sky is the ceiling above the earth.
* Shaykh: So rain descends from the lowest heaven?
* Student: From the lowest heaven.
* Shaykh: Is that what you believe?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: You are wrong in both interpretation and belief.
* Student: The sky, may Allah bless you, is the height.
* Shaykh: What is meant is the height; for it is known that rain does not descend from the lowest heaven, but descends from the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth.
Is there wisdom in Allah sending it down, i.e., the rain, from above and not...?
* Student: If rain came from the earth, the earth would be flooded and it would not reach the mountain peaks.
* Shaykh: Yes, so it has wisdom, to irrigate the earth, its upper and lower parts. Correct.
Is there wisdom in Allah making it drops?
* Student: So that the earth does not flood.
* Shaykh: No, it would flood even if it were drops.
* Student: So that buildings are not destroyed.
* Shaykh: Yes, so that the earth is not corrupted and buildings are not destroyed; if it descended like the mouths of waterskins, the earth would be corrupted, but it is from Allah's wisdom that He sent it down in drops.
Allah, Most High, said: ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a part﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 15]. ﴿They have made﴾: the pronoun refers to the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians. ﴿for Him﴾: i.e., for Allah. ﴿from His servants﴾: i.e., His creatures. ﴿a part﴾: i.e., a portion; this is due to the polytheists' saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah, the Jews' saying that 'Uzayr is the son of Allah, and the Christians' saying that the Messiah is the son of Allah.
The reason it is a "part" is that a child is a part of its father, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said about his daughter Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her: "She is a piece of my flesh; what troubles her troubles me,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5230) and Muslim (2449/93), with the wording: "My daughter is only a piece of me; what troubles her troubles me, and what harms her harms me."]] when people spoke that Ali ibn Abi Talib wanted to marry Abu Jahl's daughter as a second wife, and the Prophet (ﷺ) disapproved and said: it is not possible for the daughter of the Messenger of Allah to be with the daughter of the enemy of Allah.[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (3729) from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah who said: Ali proposed to Abu Jahl's daughter, and Fatimah heard of it and came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: Your people claim you do not get angry for your daughters, and this Ali is marrying Abu Jahl's daughter. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up, and I heard him when he gave the testimony, saying: "As for what follows, I gave in marriage Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi', and he spoke to me and was truthful. Fatimah is a piece of me, and I dislike that she be hurt. By Allah, the daughter of the Messenger of Allah and the daughter of the enemy of Allah shall not be united under one man."]]
So "part" means portion, and the speakers are three groups of people: the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians.
﴿Indeed, mankind is clearly ungrateful﴾: ﴿Indeed, mankind﴾ means the genus; ﴿clearly ungrateful﴾: i.e., manifestly ungrateful. This is because (bāna) meaning (ẓahara, to become apparent) may be with a hamza or without; so it is permissible linguistically to say: bāna al-fajr and abāna al-fajr. Accordingly, ﴿mubīn﴾ means: clearly disbelieving. There is no doubt that one who says the angels are the daughters of Allah, or Jesus is the son of Allah, or 'Uzayr is the son of Allah, has undoubtedly disbelieved in a manifest way. (abāna) with hamza is used transitively, as one says: abāna al-shay', meaning: he made it manifest.
From it is His saying: ﴿Ha Mim. By the clear Book﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 1–2], which was mentioned at the beginning of the surah; i.e., the one that makes the realities manifest and clarifies them.
Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Or has He taken from what He creates daughters and chosen you for sons?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 16]. (Am) here is disjunctive, meaning: rather, along with the interrogative hamza.
Know that (am) comes connected when it is between two equal things, and disconnected when what follows it is cut off from what precedes it. In His saying: ﴿And it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [Ya-Sin 10], what is this?
* Student: Connected.
* Shaykh: Connected. In a verse like this, (am) is disjunctive. Grammarians estimate the disjunctive (am) as (bal and the hamza): (bal, do they take...).
* Student: (Am: meaning the interrogative hamza of denunciation, with an implied saying; i.e., do you say "He has taken daughters from what He creates" for Himself, "and chosen you" "for sons," which is the necessary implication of your previous saying, so it is among the denounced things.)
* Shaykh: ﴿Or has He taken from what He creates daughters﴾ the author estimated it as: (rather, do they say...), but there is no need for this estimation; rather it is speech from Allah which He denounces against these people: i.e., rather, against your saying "He has taken from what He creates daughters," for they said the angels are the daughters of Allah.
﴿And chosen you for sons﴾: i.e., He has preferred you with sons and singled you out with them; for they say: the daughters are for Allah and the sons are for us. Is this justice? Is this right? This is a denounced injustice; at the very least, if they had said they are equal, it would have been more tolerable though still denounced; but they assign to Allah daughters and for themselves what they desire. This is the utmost of injustice and oppression.
﴿Or has He taken from what He creates daughters﴾: these are the angels whom they claimed to be daughters of Allah; ﴿and chosen you for sons﴾: so the hamza implied is for denunciation.
* From these two verses are benefits, among them: a child is a part of his father, as in His saying: ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a part﴾; therefore in inheritance by agnatic residue the son takes precedence over the father; i.e., if a man dies leaving a father and a son, the father receives a sixth as a fixed share, and the remainder goes to the son as agnate. So the son's share is now five-sixths and the father's share is one-sixth. Why?
Because the son is a part of his father, so he is given precedence.
* Among the benefits: it is permissible for a father to take from his child's property, because the child is a part of him; and when he is a part of him he is like the rest of his body. Hence a hadith says: "You and your property belong to your father." So the father may take from his child's property as he wishes, on condition that the child does not need it or that his own soul is attached to it.
For example: if the son has a female slave whom he has taken as a concubine and to whom his soul is attached, the father may not take possession of her, even though he cannot have intercourse with her because she is his son's wife; but not even taking possession. Why? Because his need is attached to her.
Likewise, if something is attached to his property by necessity, such as a son who has money set aside for his dowry when he marries, the father may not take any of it; likewise if he has a car prepared for his need and necessity, the father may not take possession of it, but may take only the surplus. The proof of this is the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "There shall be no harm and no reciprocating harm."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the exposure of the arrogance of the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians, in that they made Him who did not beget, was not begotten, and to whom no one is equal, into a father.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verse 15–16 (part 2 of 2):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: man by his nature is "clearly ungrateful" (kafur mubin). This is if we take (al-insan, "man") in the generic sense. If we take (al-insan) to refer back to ﴿They have attributed to Him from His servants a portion﴾, then it is specific. But the first meaning is apparent from the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they declined to bear it and feared it, and man bore it. Indeed, he was ever unjust and ignorant﴾ [al-Ahzab 72]. So the origin of man is injustice and ignorance, unless Allah bestows upon him knowledge and faith.
* Among the benefits of the second verse: the rebuke of those who attributed a son to Allah, as shown by His saying: ﴿Has He taken daughters from what He creates?﴾
* Among its benefits: how can the created be a son of the Creator? For this reason He said: ﴿from what He creates daughters﴾. This is impossible, because the created is separate and distinct from the Creator, so it is not valid for it to be His son.
* Among the benefits of this verse: an indication of the injustice of those who said that the angels are daughters of Allah, as shown by His saying: ﴿and has chosen for you sons?﴾, meaning: can this be conceived?!
﴿And when one of them is given good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾ ﴿And when one of them is given good news﴾ means by this the Quraysh and those like them who dislike daughters and bury them alive. ﴿And when one of them is given good news﴾, i.e., he is informed that a daughter has been born to him, his face becomes dark.
His saying here: ﴿of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness﴾, and not as He said in the second verse: ﴿And when one of them is given good news of a female﴾ [al-Nahl 58], is because what preceded it was the mention of their saying that the angels are daughters of Allah, so they made it a likeness for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: when one of them is given good news of this that they have made a likeness for the Most Merciful, ﴿his face becomes dark﴾, i.e., his face becomes dark. And (ẓalla) here is with the dotted ẓā’ because it means "became"; whereas (ḍalla) with the ṣād means "went astray and was lost." You say: "ḍalla al-ṭarīq," meaning he lost his way and lost it. As for ﴿ẓalla wajhuhu musawwadan﴾, it means "his face became dark," i.e., after it had been white. And His saying: ﴿and he is filled with suppressed grief﴾ means: filled with rage and sorrow.

* Shaykh: It means: We rendered it. Sometimes (ja'ala) means ṣayyara (to render), and sometimes means khalaqa (to create), according to context; if it governs two objects it means ṣayyara, and if it governs one object it means khalaqa, like the Most High's saying: ﴿And He made the darknesses and the light﴾ [Al-An'am 1]; this is in the sense of khalaqa, because it governs only one object. But if it governs two objects, it means ṣayyara.
* Student: Shaykh, His saying: ﴿So that you may be guided﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 10]; the intended guidance is the guidance of the roads, as you mentioned, Your Eminence. Can it be interpreted as the guidance of taking lesson from the verse?
* Shaykh: No; the basis of this prevents it.
* Student: Shaykh, regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾, there are some words in the Qur'an whose origin is foreign (...)?
* Shaykh: This one asks: despite ﴿Indeed, We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾, there are some words in the Qur'an whose origin is not Arabic. We say: when the Arabs spoke them they became Arabic through usage, even if their origin is not Arabic.
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a part. Indeed, mankind is clearly ungrateful (15). Or has He taken from what He creates daughters and chosen you for sons? (16) And when one of them is given good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful, his face becomes darkened, and he suppresses grief (17). Is one who is brought up in ornaments and is in dispute not clear? (18). And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, females. Did they witness their creation? Their testimony will be recorded, and they will be questioned﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 15–19].
* Shaykh: All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah send blessings and peace upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family, companions, and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.
To proceed: the interpretation of the Great Qur'an is among the most important duties of Muslims, that they understand the meaning of the speech of Allah, Glorified and Exalted; for speech whose meaning is not understood is not benefited from, and one who reads without understanding is like the unlettered who does not read, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And among them are unlettered ones who do not know the Book except wishful thinking﴾ [Al-Baqarah 78]; i.e., except recitation, so Allah named them unlettered.
The Qur'an is explained by the Qur'an; if not, then by the Sunnah; if not, then by the sayings of the Companions, especially those well known for knowledge of tafsir; if not, then by what the senior Successors among the people of tafsir said. This is the principle followed by the People of the Sunnah and the Community.
As for interpretation by opinion (ra'y), some who do it are mistaken and some are correct, but it is not permissible for a person to interpret the Qur'an by his opinion, meaning to bend the Qur'an to his opinion; for whoever speaks about the Qur'an by his opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire.
An example of that: those who interpret the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched﴾ [Al-Ma'idah 64] as meaning bounty. These have spoken about the Qur'an by their opinion, because this meaning is definitely not what is intended. Likewise those who say ﴿He istawa over the Throne﴾ [Al-A'raf 54] means He seized control of the Throne; this is a reprehensible statement, and interpreting the verse thus is speaking about Allah without knowledge, a fabrication against Allah, Glorified and Exalted.
We say of these that they spoke about the Qur'an by their opinion; i.e., they bent the Qur'an to their opinion. As for one who interprets the Qur'an according to the established legal and linguistic realities, when there is no legal technical meaning, he has not spoken about the Qur'an by his opinion.
This principle was already mentioned when we first began the science of tafsir, so let it be a reference for you. Is the Qur'an interpreted first by...?
* Students: By the Qur'an.
* Shaykh: Then?
* Students: By the Sunnah.
* Shaykh: Then?
* Students: By the sayings of the Companions.
* Shaykh: Then?
* Students: The senior Successors.
* Shaykh: The senior Successors who gave attention to tafsir, such as Mujahid ibn Jabr, may Allah have mercy on him, who took tafsir from Abdullah ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him.
We previously noted in tafsir that Allah, Most High, analogized the unseen to the seen. What is that?
* Student: His saying, Most High: ﴿Thus you will be brought forth﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 11].
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: He analogized the seen, which is the giving of life...
* Shaykh: No, what is the seen? He analogized the unseen, which is the reviving of the dead, to the seen that they witness: He sent down water from the sky and with it brought forth every fruit. So He analogized the future to the present, and this is one of the methods of teaching and making understood.
His saying: ﴿Water from the sky﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 11]; what is meant by "sky"?
* Student: The sky is the ceiling above the earth.
* Shaykh: So rain descends from the lowest heaven?
* Student: From the lowest heaven.
* Shaykh: Is that what you believe?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: You are wrong in both interpretation and belief.
* Student: The sky, may Allah bless you, is the height.
* Shaykh: What is meant is the height; for it is known that rain does not descend from the lowest heaven, but descends from the clouds subjected between the sky and the earth.
Is there wisdom in Allah sending it down, i.e., the rain, from above and not...?
* Student: If rain came from the earth, the earth would be flooded and it would not reach the mountain peaks.
* Shaykh: Yes, so it has wisdom, to irrigate the earth, its upper and lower parts. Correct.
Is there wisdom in Allah making it drops?
* Student: So that the earth does not flood.
* Shaykh: No, it would flood even if it were drops.
* Student: So that buildings are not destroyed.
* Shaykh: Yes, so that the earth is not corrupted and buildings are not destroyed; if it descended like the mouths of waterskins, the earth would be corrupted, but it is from Allah's wisdom that He sent it down in drops.
Allah, Most High, said: ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a part﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 15]. ﴿They have made﴾: the pronoun refers to the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians. ﴿for Him﴾: i.e., for Allah. ﴿from His servants﴾: i.e., His creatures. ﴿a part﴾: i.e., a portion; this is due to the polytheists' saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah, the Jews' saying that 'Uzayr is the son of Allah, and the Christians' saying that the Messiah is the son of Allah.
The reason it is a "part" is that a child is a part of its father, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said about his daughter Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her: "She is a piece of my flesh; what troubles her troubles me,"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (5230) and Muslim (2449/93), with the wording: "My daughter is only a piece of me; what troubles her troubles me, and what harms her harms me."]] when people spoke that Ali ibn Abi Talib wanted to marry Abu Jahl's daughter as a second wife, and the Prophet (ﷺ) disapproved and said: it is not possible for the daughter of the Messenger of Allah to be with the daughter of the enemy of Allah.[[Recorded by al-Bukhari (3729) from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah who said: Ali proposed to Abu Jahl's daughter, and Fatimah heard of it and came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: Your people claim you do not get angry for your daughters, and this Ali is marrying Abu Jahl's daughter. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood up, and I heard him when he gave the testimony, saying: "As for what follows, I gave in marriage Abu al-As ibn al-Rabi', and he spoke to me and was truthful. Fatimah is a piece of me, and I dislike that she be hurt. By Allah, the daughter of the Messenger of Allah and the daughter of the enemy of Allah shall not be united under one man."]]
So "part" means portion, and the speakers are three groups of people: the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians.
﴿Indeed, mankind is clearly ungrateful﴾: ﴿Indeed, mankind﴾ means the genus; ﴿clearly ungrateful﴾: i.e., manifestly ungrateful. This is because (bāna) meaning (ẓahara, to become apparent) may be with a hamza or without; so it is permissible linguistically to say: bāna al-fajr and abāna al-fajr. Accordingly, ﴿mubīn﴾ means: clearly disbelieving. There is no doubt that one who says the angels are the daughters of Allah, or Jesus is the son of Allah, or 'Uzayr is the son of Allah, has undoubtedly disbelieved in a manifest way. (abāna) with hamza is used transitively, as one says: abāna al-shay', meaning: he made it manifest.
From it is His saying: ﴿Ha Mim. By the clear Book﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 1–2], which was mentioned at the beginning of the surah; i.e., the one that makes the realities manifest and clarifies them.
Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Or has He taken from what He creates daughters and chosen you for sons?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 16]. (Am) here is disjunctive, meaning: rather, along with the interrogative hamza.
Know that (am) comes connected when it is between two equal things, and disconnected when what follows it is cut off from what precedes it. In His saying: ﴿And it is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them﴾ [Ya-Sin 10], what is this?
* Student: Connected.
* Shaykh: Connected. In a verse like this, (am) is disjunctive. Grammarians estimate the disjunctive (am) as (bal and the hamza): (bal, do they take...).
* Student: (Am: meaning the interrogative hamza of denunciation, with an implied saying; i.e., do you say "He has taken daughters from what He creates" for Himself, "and chosen you" "for sons," which is the necessary implication of your previous saying, so it is among the denounced things.)
* Shaykh: ﴿Or has He taken from what He creates daughters﴾ the author estimated it as: (rather, do they say...), but there is no need for this estimation; rather it is speech from Allah which He denounces against these people: i.e., rather, against your saying "He has taken from what He creates daughters," for they said the angels are the daughters of Allah.
﴿And chosen you for sons﴾: i.e., He has preferred you with sons and singled you out with them; for they say: the daughters are for Allah and the sons are for us. Is this justice? Is this right? This is a denounced injustice; at the very least, if they had said they are equal, it would have been more tolerable though still denounced; but they assign to Allah daughters and for themselves what they desire. This is the utmost of injustice and oppression.
﴿Or has He taken from what He creates daughters﴾: these are the angels whom they claimed to be daughters of Allah; ﴿and chosen you for sons﴾: so the hamza implied is for denunciation.
* From these two verses are benefits, among them: a child is a part of his father, as in His saying: ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a part﴾; therefore in inheritance by agnatic residue the son takes precedence over the father; i.e., if a man dies leaving a father and a son, the father receives a sixth as a fixed share, and the remainder goes to the son as agnate. So the son's share is now five-sixths and the father's share is one-sixth. Why?
Because the son is a part of his father, so he is given precedence.
* Among the benefits: it is permissible for a father to take from his child's property, because the child is a part of him; and when he is a part of him he is like the rest of his body. Hence a hadith says: "You and your property belong to your father." So the father may take from his child's property as he wishes, on condition that the child does not need it or that his own soul is attached to it.
For example: if the son has a female slave whom he has taken as a concubine and to whom his soul is attached, the father may not take possession of her, even though he cannot have intercourse with her because she is his son's wife; but not even taking possession. Why? Because his need is attached to her.
Likewise, if something is attached to his property by necessity, such as a son who has money set aside for his dowry when he marries, the father may not take any of it; likewise if he has a car prepared for his need and necessity, the father may not take possession of it, but may take only the surplus. The proof of this is the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "There shall be no harm and no reciprocating harm."
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the exposure of the arrogance of the polytheists, the Jews, and the Christians, in that they made Him who did not beget, was not begotten, and to whom no one is equal, into a father.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verse 15–16 (part 2 of 2):

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: man by his nature is "clearly ungrateful" (kafur mubin). This is if we take (al-insan, "man") in the generic sense. If we take (al-insan) to refer back to ﴿They have attributed to Him from His servants a portion﴾, then it is specific. But the first meaning is apparent from the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, but they declined to bear it and feared it, and man bore it. Indeed, he was ever unjust and ignorant﴾ [al-Ahzab 72]. So the origin of man is injustice and ignorance, unless Allah bestows upon him knowledge and faith.
* Among the benefits of the second verse: the rebuke of those who attributed a son to Allah, as shown by His saying: ﴿Has He taken daughters from what He creates?﴾
* Among its benefits: how can the created be a son of the Creator? For this reason He said: ﴿from what He creates daughters﴾. This is impossible, because the created is separate and distinct from the Creator, so it is not valid for it to be His son.
* Among the benefits of this verse: an indication of the injustice of those who said that the angels are daughters of Allah, as shown by His saying: ﴿and has chosen for you sons?﴾, meaning: can this be conceived?!
﴿And when one of them is given good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness, his face becomes dark, and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾ ﴿And when one of them is given good news﴾ means by this the Quraysh and those like them who dislike daughters and bury them alive. ﴿And when one of them is given good news﴾, i.e., he is informed that a daughter has been born to him, his face becomes dark.
His saying here: ﴿of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness﴾, and not as He said in the second verse: ﴿And when one of them is given good news of a female﴾ [al-Nahl 58], is because what preceded it was the mention of their saying that the angels are daughters of Allah, so they made it a likeness for Allah, the Mighty and Majestic: when one of them is given good news of this that they have made a likeness for the Most Merciful, ﴿his face becomes dark﴾, i.e., his face becomes dark. And (ẓalla) here is with the dotted ẓā’ because it means "became"; whereas (ḍalla) with the ṣād means "went astray and was lost." You say: "ḍalla al-ṭarīq," meaning he lost his way and lost it. As for ﴿ẓalla wajhuhu musawwadan﴾, it means "his face became dark," i.e., after it had been white. And His saying: ﴿and he is filled with suppressed grief﴾ means: filled with rage and sorrow.

Student: (﴿When one of them is given good news of what he attributes to the Most Merciful as an example, his face darkens and he is filled with suppressed grief.﴾) He has made for Him a likeness through attributing daughters to Him, because the offspring resembles the parent. The meaning: when one of them is informed that a daughter has been born to him, ﴿his face became﴾ turned, ﴿darkened﴾ changed in the manner of one distressed, ﴿while he suppresses [his grief]﴾ filled with sorrow. So how can daughters be attributed to Him? He is exalted above that.

* The Shaykh: This is the meaning of what we have discussed.

* Among the benefits of this verse: it mentions the state of these people when they are given the good news of daughters: that a person among them has his outward and inward appearance changed. Outwardly, his face darkens; inwardly, he is filled with grief.

* Among them: a complete condemnation of these people, since when they are given the good news of a female, this state comes over them, yet they attribute such things to the Creator, mighty and majestic.

* And among the benefits of this noble verse: the affirmation of the name ar-Rahman for Allah, mighty and majestic. Ar-Rahman means the One possessing vast mercy. The Quraysh denied this noble name: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful?"﴾ [al-Furqan 60]. When the Prophet (ﷺ) wanted to write the treaty of peace at Hudaybiyah and said to the scribe, "Write: In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate," the representative of Quraysh refused and said, "We do not recognize the Most Merciful; rather, write: In Your name, O Allah." The Prophet (ﷺ) then said, "Write: In Your name, O Allah."[[The lengthy hadith of the treaty of Hudaybiyah was narrated by al-Bukhari (2731) from the hadith of al-Miswar ibn Makhramah (may Allah be pleased with him).]]

This was not a matter of conceding, but a matter of concluding the agreement and completing the pact.

We said that ar-Rahman means the One possessing vast mercy. Does the mercy of Allah, mighty and majestic, include the disbelievers?

The answer: Yes. Were it not for the mercy of Allah, no disbeliever would remain even for a moment. The disbeliever is shown mercy, and the believer is shown mercy, but the difference is that the believer is shown mercy in this world and the Hereafter, while the disbeliever is shown mercy in this world only: Allah has lavished blessings upon him and hastened good things for him, but in the Hereafter he will be treated with justice and recompensed according to what he deserves.
