So we say: general mercy includes the believer and the disbeliever, and specific mercy is restricted to the believers.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the change of the complexion according to what pleases or displeases. When a person is given good news that pleases him, his face shines with joy, and you perceive that he is pleased by it, and the reverse is also true.

* Branching from this benefit: the body follows the heart. When the heart is illuminated and rejoices, the body does likewise, and the reverse is also true.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the polytheists are not content with Allah's decree. They change outwardly and inwardly: outwardly by the darkening of their faces, and inwardly by being filled with grief.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verse 18:

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Is one who is brought up among ornaments, and who in dispute is not clear [in expression]?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 18]. The hamza is the interrogative particle, the waw is a conjunction, and "man" (who) is a relative pronoun; meaning: "or the one who." ﴿Is brought up among ornaments﴾ means: is raised with them and has need of them. ﴿And in dispute is not clear﴾ means: does not make clear what is in himself; meaning: like one who is not like that. The indication in this description is to the female, because the female is brought up among ornaments and adorned to beautify herself, so she needs that which completes her; and she is also not one of disputation, rather in dispute she is not clear, like one who is not like that?

* Student: O Shaykh, may Allah preserve you, is it permissible to interpret the Qur'an by what is known as scientific miracles from the Qur'an and Sunnah?

* The Shaykh: Scientific miracles are of two types:

One type is indicated by the Qur'an and pointed to by it; this is not objectionable, and it is part of the interpretation of the Qur'an.

The other type is not indicated by the Qur'an, but is derived from it with strain, and perhaps is not indicated at all; it is not permissible to interpret the Qur'an by this.

An example of that: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿O assembly of jinn and mankind, if you are able to pass beyond the regions of the heavens and the earth, then pass; you will not pass except with authority﴾ [al-Rahman 33]. Some of them interpreted it as referring to science and applied it to reaching the moon. This is not permissible, because the verse does not indicate that. The verse contains a description of the state on the Day of Resurrection, and for this reason He said: ﴿from the regions of the heavens and the earth﴾, and it is known that these people did not pass beyond the regions of the heavens. So scientific miracles that involve no strain are not objectionable, because the Qur'an is broad.

Among what is also rejected, from what is called scientific miracles, is what they call the numerical miracle based on nineteen. This too is false, and it is not permissible to say that the Qur'an is miraculous from this aspect.

Firstly: because the readings differ, and they say, for example, the letter ta' is repeated such-and-such a number of times; if you divide it by nineteen it divides evenly; the letter lam is repeated such-and-such a number of times; if you divide it by nineteen it divides without remainder.

Thus they claim, and this is without doubt false. Some of them even said to me: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran 96], and He said in Surah al-Fath: ﴿And it is He who withheld their hands from you and your hands from them within the valley of Makkah﴾ [al-Fath 24]. He said: Allah mentioned "Bakkah" so that the letter ba' would complete the number that divides by nineteen. This is without doubt a lie.

The proof: for example, there are words in the Qur'an that have variant readings: ﴿O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient one with a report, then investigate﴾ [al-Hujurat 6]; there is a reading ﴿fa-tathabbatu﴾ (then verify), so the count is disrupted: the nun is replaced by a tha' and the ya' by a ba'.

Likewise ﴿Master of the Day of Judgement﴾ [al-Fatihah 4], and there is a reading ﴿Malik yawm al-din﴾ with the alif omitted, so the alif is lost.

The point is that this is without doubt a lie, and it is not permissible to interpret the Qur'an by the numerical miracle; because, firstly, there is no miracle in it as they claim; and secondly, the Qur'an was not revealed as a mathematical exercise, but was revealed as an admonition and a healing for what is in the breasts.

* Student: O our Shaykh, may Allah preserve you, the one who launched this innovation was a man who denied the second part of the testimony, and said that the testimony is limited only to "There is no god but Allah."

* The Shaykh: In any case, we do not know of his condition except what you have just mentioned. He is a man, I think, named Rashad, and he spread this some years ago, but he was killed; some people killed him because he innovated in the religion of Allah what is not part of it. But these last days I found a person with him holding a page of this type, wanting to print it at his own expense and distribute it among people. I said to him: this is not permissible, and I tore up the paper he had given me, and I said: you must know that the Qur'an was only revealed to reform creation, not to test their minds with numbers and the like. Then, as you have heard now, there are verses that differ, which prevent this composition that he mentioned.

* Student: O Shaykh, may Allah reward you well, ﴿his face remains darkened﴾ [al-Zukhruf 17]: is this in this world and the Hereafter, or in this world?

* The Shaykh: In this world.

* Student: O Shaykh, may Allah preserve you, now there are papers, for example, that say: the number of letters of the Mushaf is such-and-such; so if you read the entire Mushaf, you multiply it by ten, and it says: you will have such-and-such a number of good deeds, and if you read...?

* The Shaykh: This is a lie. Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, passed by a people who were glorifying Allah and counting with pebbles, and he said to them: you will never count your deeds. Your good deeds are counted for you and written down; but count your evil deeds, so that you may repent to Allah from them. This is true. All these things that I have mentioned and that you have mentioned are innovations, and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, does not waste the reward of anyone; He knows the number of the letters of the Qur'an and knows what follows from it of reward, and it will not be lost.

* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. ﴿And they say: If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them. They have no knowledge of that; they are only guessing. Or have We given them a Book before this, so that they are holding to it? Rather, they say: Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are guided by their footsteps. And likewise, We did not send before you any warner into a city except that its affluent ones said: Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps﴾ [al-Zukhruf 20–23].
* The Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan. It has passed that Allah, Glorified and Exalted, denounced those who attributed daughters to Allah and attributed sons to themselves, and He said: ﴿And they have made for Him from His servants a portion. Indeed, mankind is clearly ungrateful﴾ [al-Zukhruf 15]. So what is "a portion"?

* Student: That is: a child (son).

* The Shaykh: In what sense is a child a portion? What is the evidence?

* Student: The evidence is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to Fatimah: "She is a part of me."

* The Shaykh: "A part of me," like this?

* Student: "A piece of flesh of mine" ("بضعة مني").

* The Shaykh: "A piece of flesh of mine"[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3714) and Muslim (2449/94), from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, may Allah be pleased with him.]], yes.

His saying: ﴿And when one of them is given good tidings of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as an example﴾. What is it that he attributed to the Most Merciful as an example?

* Student: They said: the Most Merciful took daughters from among the angels.

* The Shaykh: ﴿That which he attributes to the Most Merciful as an example﴾; i.e., He made them.

* Student: That is: He made daughters for Himself and sons for them.

* The Shaykh: A likeness to Him, since they claimed that the angels are daughters of Allah.

(Kazim) — what is its meaning?

* Student: Kazim: filled with rage.

* The Shaykh: Filled with rage. So his outward appearance changes?

* Student: And his inward.

* The Shaykh: His outward appearance changes in what way?

* Student: By the change of his complexion.

* The Shaykh: Yes, his face remains darkened. And his inward?

* Student: With grief.

* The Shaykh: He said: ﴿Is one who is brought up among ornaments, and who in dispute is not clear?﴾ [al-Zukhruf 18]. ﴿Is one who⦆ — the hamza is interrogative, the waw is a conjunction, and "man" means "the one who"; the meaning: or the one who is raised. The meaning of ﴿is raised﴾ is: is brought up. And ﴿among ornaments﴾: the commentator said: (i.e., adornment). ﴿And in dispute﴾: in disputation. (﴿is not clear﴾: does not make clear the argument, because of her weakness in it due to being female.) This is the tafsir.

﴿Or who⦆: he says: (the hamza is for denial, the waw for conjunction with a clause, i.e., "Do they attribute to Allah one who is raised...") meaning that the conjunction here is on the presumption of: they attribute. Where is the correlative left for us? The correlative: "like one who is not like that."

﴿Or is one who is brought up among ornaments and who in dispute is not clear﴾ means: the woman is not beautiful in herself, but is in need of what beautifies her; for this reason you find among women fashions; they have no concern except fashions, beautification and embellishment, and the like. Why? Because she is deficient in herself.

Likewise also, in her speech she is deficient: ﴿and in dispute is not clear﴾; in disputation she is overcome, not making clear the argument, because she is weak by reason of being female. What remains: what is the counterpart? ﴿Or is one who is brought up﴾ — there must be a counterpart. What is it? Answer, all of you.

* Students: "Like one who is not like that."

* The Shaykh: Like one who does not need to be raised among ornaments, and like one who in dispute is clear, and that is the male. The meaning: Allah adds blame to blame upon these people, in that they attribute to Allah what is deficient in its speech and its deeds, and attribute to themselves what is perfect.

* In this verse there are benefits, among them: the deficiency of woman, and that she can never equal man in her intellect and her guidance, by His saying: ﴿Or is one who is brought up among ornaments﴾ to the end.

* And among them: that woman has no concern except beautification and care for her appearance.

* And among them: that woman is not one of disputation; rather she is weak and cannot dispute, nor make clear what is in her heart of argument. For this reason, when the daughter of Kisra took over the Persians, and that reached the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, he said: "A people will never prosper who entrust their affair to a woman." People differed over the meaning of his saying: "A people will never prosper who entrust their affair to a woman": is this specific to this particular case, meaning that these people will not prosper because they entrusted their affair to a woman, or is it general for every people who entrust their affair to a woman?

If we look at the generality, "A people will never prosper who entrust their affair to a woman," we say: this is general for every people who entrust their affair to a woman; and if we look at the specific case, we say: it is specific.

And if we look at reality, does a woman who takes charge of men's affairs prosper?

The answer: if she prospers, that is by the help of men, or it is a relative prosperity. For example, a woman who is a prime minister will not prosper; her people will not prosper except through men supporting her. That is one point.

Or it may be said: it is a relative prosperity; if someone other than her, a man, had taken charge, that would have been more prosperous for them.

Likewise, they will not prosper if they entrust their affair to a woman in other than leadership, such as the ministry, for example; they will not prosper.

And whoever knows women and their frequent disputes and problems, even when they take charge of the administration of a school, knows that a woman is in no way suitable for authority, except over her own sex, and even that perhaps, because the weak is for the weak.

* Among the benefits of this verse: praise of men, because if women are not complete in themselves, neither in deeds nor in speech, this means that men are complete. Consider the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And Mary, daughter of 'Imran, who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her of Our Spirit, and she believed in the words of her Lord and His scriptures, and she was of the devoutly obedient﴾ [al-Tahrim 12]. Is it "of the devoutly obedient" (men) or "of the devoutly obedient women"?

* Student: "of the devoutly obedient" (al-qanitin).

* The Shaykh: "of the devoutly obedient" (al-qanitin). It becomes clear to you that devotion and worship are more among men, and for this reason it came in the hadith: "Many among men have attained perfection, but among women none have attained perfection except four: Asiyah the wife of Pharaoh, Mary daughter of 'Imran, Khadijah daughter of Khuwaylid, and Fatimah daughter of Muhammad. And the excellence of 'A'ishah over women is like the excellence of tharid over all other food."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3769) and Muslim (2431/70) from the hadith of Abu Musa, with the wording: "Many among men have attained perfection, but among women none have attained perfection except Mary daughter of 'Imran and Asiyah the wife of Pharaoh. And the excess of 'A'ishah over women is like the excess of tharid over other food." Al-Tha'labi also narrated it in his tafsir 9/353 from Abu Musa, with the wording: "Many among men have attained perfection, but among women none have attained perfection except four: Asiyah daughter of Muzahim the wife of Pharaoh, Mary daughter of 'Imran, Khadijah daughter of Khuwaylid, and Fatimah daughter of Muhammad. And the excess of 'A'ishah over women is like the excess of tharid over other food."]]

All of this we want to remain in our minds: that woman is deficient, and that those who try to make her like men are opposed to the natural disposition and nature, as they are opposed to the Shari'ah.

The Prophet ﷺ addressed the women on a day of 'Eid, a day of joy and happiness, and clarified their condition, saying: "I have not seen anyone deficient in intellect and religion who takes away the mind of a firm man more than one of you."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (304) from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with him.]] Although it was a day of joy and happiness, it would have been expected that the Prophet ﷺ would bring happiness, but he had to clarify their condition.

Now those people among the disbelievers and others who have equated women with men in most matters, their conditions are not upright and not complete, although they will never be able to bring women up to men in every respect; never, that is impossible.

[Allah] said: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf 19]. "(They made)": the pronoun refers to the polytheists. The meaning of "made" (ja'alū) is "rendered" (ṣayyarū), which is why it takes two objects. ﴿The angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful﴾, who have fulfilled servanthood in its most perfect form, since Allah, Exalted is He, described them as honored servants who do not speak before Him and act only by His command. ﴿Females﴾, and this is by their saying: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." Consider this fabrication. First, they fabricated that they are the daughters of Allah. Second, they fabricated that they are females. How do they know that the angels are daughters? But since the attribute of femaleness is a deficient attribute, they said: "They are females." And the sons, for whom are they? The sons are for them.

Allah, Exalted is He, said, disapproving of them: ﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ That is: were they present at their creation and did they know that they are females? The interrogative here is for denial or for challenge; that is, Allah denied against them, or challenged them, whether they were present or not. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor the creation of themselves, and I would not take misleaders as helpers﴾ [al-Kahf 51].

Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Their testimony will be recorded﴾ that they are females. ﴿Will be recorded﴾: it is recorded as a fabrication and false testimony, and they will be punished for it. The "sīn" here is for proximity and certainty. "Will be recorded" does not specify the agent of the writing, so Allah knows best: will Allah record it, or the angels? The apparent meaning is that it is the angels, because the angels are assigned to record the deeds of the children of Adam: ﴿Not a word does he utter but there is with him an watchful observer, ready﴾ [Qaf 18].

(﴿Their testimony will be recorded﴾ that they are females, ﴿and they will be questioned﴾ about it in the Hereafter, and punishment will follow from it.)

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: demonstrating the fabrication of these polytheists in two respects. The first respect?

* Student: That they made the angels females.

* The Shaykh: The first respect: they, the angels themselves, made the angels females, and how do they know?!

The second respect?

* Student: They said: the angels are the daughters of Allah.

* The Shaykh: Yes, they attributed them to Allah, Exalted is He.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the challenge to these fabricators. The challenge to these fabricators is by what?

* Student: When they mentioned the angels as females.

* The Shaykh: How? By which expression do we know that it is a challenge to them? Where is the word that indicates the challenge?

* Student: ﴿The servants of the Most Merciful﴾.

* Another student: Allah said: ﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾

* The Shaykh: In His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾. And the answer is: no.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: a warning to those fabricators that their testimony will be recorded and they will be punished for it, based on His saying: ﴿Their testimony will be recorded﴾.

* And among the benefits of the verse: the affirmation of accountability in His saying: ﴿and they will be questioned﴾.

* And among the benefits of this verse: that a person's statements are recorded against him just as his actions are, because the testimony here is by speech.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verse 20:

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And they say, "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them."﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 20], (﴿we would not have worshipped them﴾ means: the angels. So our worship of them is by His will, and He is pleased with it. Allah the Exalted said) to the end.

﴿And they say﴾, i.e., the polytheists, ﴿"If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them"﴾. (Law) here is a particle of negation of a negation (law shāʾa Allāh mā ʿabadnāhum: "if Allah had willed, we would not have worshipped them"), meaning: we worshipped them because Allah willed it.

It is strange that they said: ﴿we would not have worshipped them﴾. If they mean the angels, then they have contradicted themselves. If they mean the idols, then this has a different discussion. If they mean the angels, they said ﴿them﴾ although they had made the angels females, and the expected form would have been: "we would not have worshipped them [feminine]", so that the pronoun returns to the angels as a feminine pronoun. But if what they intend by ﴿we would not have worshipped them﴾ is "we would not have worshipped our gods", then there is no difficulty.

Which view did the exegete (mufassir) take?

What is the difficulty in His words ﴿we would not have worshipped them﴾, and what is the nature of the difficulty in it?

* Student: The difficulty is that if what is meant is the angels, then they have contradicted themselves.

* Shaykh: If they mean the angels, they have contradicted themselves.

* Student: That is, they made them females, and the pronoun "them" refers to the angels.

* Shaykh: It refers to the angels, well done. And if it refers to the idols?

* Student: Then there is no difficulty.

* Shaykh: Then there is no difficulty.

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾ (﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾: the saying, regarding being pleased with their worship; ﴿knowledge﴾; ﴿They are only﴾, i.e., they are not, ﴿but guessing﴾: lying, and so punishment is due to them for it).

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾. The word (min) here is parsed as an extra particle grammatically (ziyādah iʿrāban), but in meaning it is useful, conveying emphasis. The context of the speech, were it not for the Qur'an, would be: mā lahum bi-dhālika ʿilm ("they have no knowledge of that"), but particles are added for emphasis, to emphasise the negation in this verse. That is to say, their saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ is a statement built on conjecture, supposition, and disputation by falsehood. Otherwise, they acted and worshipped without knowing that it had been decreed for them, because what is decreed is not known except once it occurs.

* There are benefits in this verse. Among them: these people argued from predestination (al-qadar), saying: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them."

* Among them: the invalidity of arguing from predestination, by His saying: ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾.

Here is a question: is their saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ correct?

* Students: Correct.

* Shaykh: Correct, but arguing with it is not correct. "If the Most Merciful had willed, they would not have worshipped them," like His saying: ﴿And if Allah had willed, those after them would not have fought one another after the clear proofs had come to them, but they differed﴾ [Al-Baqarah 253]. So this statement is correct, but is arguing with it correct?

* Students: Not correct.

* Shaykh: Not correct. We said it is correct because Allah, the Exalted, wills everything; everything occurs by the will of Allah. But no argument may be made with something you do not know, since you do not know that this has been decreed for you except when?

* Students: When it occurs.

* Shaykh: Except when it occurs. Predestination is a hidden secret that is not known until the decreed thing occurs.

* Among the benefits of this verse: the refutation of the Qadariyya, who deny that Allah wills the actions of His servants. The Qadariyya, who are the Mu'tazila, say: man creates his own act, wills it, and is independent in it, and that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has no will concerning it. Glory be to Allah!

Does Allah, Mighty and Majestic, say: ﴿Indeed, We have created everything in measure﴾ [Al-Qamar 49], while you say: no?!

Against them stood another group, the Jabriyya, who said: everything that occurs happens by the will of Allah, and man is compelled in his action and is not free.

This is also a false view. Everyone knows the difference between a voluntary act and an involuntary act. Everyone knows the difference between a person descending from the roof by the stairs step by step and a person tumbling down without choice. They say that everything, I mean the Jabriyya, say: all is equal, whether one descends by choice or tumbles without choice; all is equal, and a person's movement is nothing but like the movement of a palm frond in the wind.

This too is a false view, and no nation can stand on it, nor any religious community, nor can worldly or otherworldly affairs be established on it. Otherwise we would say: every person would dominate another and then say, "By Allah, this is by the decree and predestination of Allah, I have no control." Would these people be content for a person to come and oppress them severely, and then say, "This is by the decree of Allah"?

* Student: No.

* Shaykh: The answer is: no. No one is content with that.

When 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu) ordered that the hand of a thief be cut off, the man said: "Gently, O Commander of the Faithful, by Allah I only stole by the decree of Allah." He said: "And we only cut off your hand by the decree of Allah." So every person knows that man is free and has complete will by which he acts.

If we said with the view of the Jabriyya, then Allah's punishment of the criminals would be injustice, because they would say: "O our Lord, we did this without choice." Those who say that Allah has no connection with the act of the servant are also mistaken, and for this reason these Qadariyya are called the Magians of this Ummah. Why? Because they made two creators for events: human events created by humans, and divine events created by Allah, Mighty and Majestic. So they were named the Magians of this Ummah, because the Magians say that events have two creators: evil is created by darkness, and good is created by light. This is the belief of the Magians. In this regard al-Mutanabbi said in praise of his patron:

How often the darkness of night has a favour from you, / Which testifies that the Manawiyya (Manichaeans) are lying.
"The darkness of night" is darkness; and you, O praised one, have generosity in the night and the day.

In any case, brothers, let us return to the verse: is their saying ﴿If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ correct or not?

* Students: Correct.

* Shaykh: Correct, but is it a proof? No. For this reason He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the one who argues by predestination has no knowledge.

How could he not have knowledge when he knows that nothing occurred except by the will of Allah? The answer: he only knows after the occurrence. But before the occurrence, does he know or not?

* Students: He does not know.

* Shaykh: He does not know. Then he has no proof, because proof is an indicator, and the indicator must precede what it indicates. Their knowledge comes after, not before.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: their saying is based on falsehood, by His saying: ﴿They are only guessing﴾; i.e., they are lying.

And we may say: ﴿guessing﴾ means "supposing," as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said in another verse: ﴿They are only supposing﴾ [Al-Jathiyah 24].

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: (﴿Or did We give them a Book before it [i.e., the Qur'an, enjoining the worship of other than Allah], so that they are holding fast to it?﴾) ﴿Or did We give them [a Book]﴾: (Am) here means (bal) (rather) together with the interrogative hamza, and the meaning is: "Rather, did We give them a Book before the Qur'an, so that they hold fast to it?" What is the answer?

* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: No, that did not happen. The first Book sent down to the Arabs was the Qur'an, and it is the last Book, because no messenger was raised from among the Arabs except Muhammad ﷺ, as the Mighty and Majestic said in the supplication of Ibrahim and Isma'il: ﴿Our Lord, and raise up among them a messenger from themselves who will recite to them Your verses and teach them the Book and wisdom﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:129].

Therefore, if someone said: "Is there among the Arabs a messenger other than Muhammad ﷺ?" we would say: "No, there is only one." ﴿Or did We give them a Book before it, so that they are holding fast to it?﴾ The answer: No.

* From the benefits of this verse: repeating the proofs in proportion to the denial of the opponent; and whenever the proofs are repeated, the matter becomes stronger.

* And from its benefits: when you have presented a convincing proof, there is no blame on you if you present a second and a third proof, as long as the situation calls for that.

Look at those who argue against the people of falsehood, especially Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah and his student Ibn al-Qayyim, how they bring proofs in succession and abundance, although the point could be established by one proof, for the sake of strengthening it. Shaykh al-Islam has a book called al-Tis'iniyyah (The Book of Ninety) in refutation of the Ash'aris who said: "Speech is the meaning standing in the soul." May Allah have mercy on him, he refuted this view in ninety ways, though one way would suffice to refute it, because whenever the proofs are repeated, the argument grows stronger.

Now consider sensory matters: if a person came and informed you of a report, and he is trustworthy in your eyes, you would accept it; if another came, your confidence would increase; and if a third came, your confidence would increase further. For this reason the scholars said: the mutawatir (widely transmitted report) conveys certainty, because of the large number of its narrators. Mutawatir means a hadith that comes through many routes, and it conveys certainty because of the multitude of narrators.

* From the benefits of this noble verse: no Book was sent down to the Arabs other than the Qur'an, due to His saying: ﴿Or did We give them a Book before it?﴾

* And from the benefits of this verse: the favour of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, upon the Arabs, in that He sent down to them one Book as guidance for all creation until the Day of Resurrection, whereas the other messengers had Books sent down to them as guidance for their own peoples, which means guidance for specific people and for a specific time. But this Book—may Allah make us and you among those who hold fast to it—is sent down, suitable for every time, place and nation.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verse 22:

Then He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Nay, but they say: "We found our fathers following a certain religion (ummah), and we are guided by following in their footsteps."﴾ [al-Zukhruf 22]. "Bal" (Nay, but) here is for idrab (a turning away, idrab intiqal: a shift to another matter), meaning they moved on to something else. "They say: We found our fathers upon an ummah," i.e., upon a millah (religion, creed), "and we are, following in their footsteps, guided," by them, and they used to worship other than Allah. This is one of their arguments. They argued with the first by what?

* Student: By predestination.

* The Shaykh: By predestination, now. They argued by following the example: ﴿They say: "We found our fathers upon an ummah, and we are guided by following in their footsteps."﴾

The verse contains many benefits, but let us discuss the meaning of (ummah). He says: (millah). We mentioned a little earlier that "ummah" in the Qur'an carries several meanings. Which one?

* Student: With the meaning of imam (leader).

* The Shaykh: It can mean imam. Give an example.

* Student: ﴿Indeed Abraham was an ummah, obedient to Allah﴾ [al-Nahl 120].

* The Shaykh: And it can mean?

* Student: It can mean a period of time (waqt).

* The Shaykh: It can mean a period of time.

* Student: ﴿And he remembered after a period (ummah)﴾ [Yusuf 45].

* The Shaykh: Due to His saying: ﴿And he remembered after a period (ummah)﴾. That is two.

* Student: It can mean a group of people (taifah).

* The Shaykh: It can mean a group of people.

* Student: Like His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every ummah a messenger﴾ [al-Nahl 36].

* The Shaykh: Like His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every ummah a messenger.﴾

* Student: With the meaning of religion (din).

* The Shaykh: With the meaning of religion. Its example?

* Student: This verse.

* The Shaykh: Which verse?

* Student: ﴿We found our fathers upon an ummah.﴾

* The Shaykh: Like His saying: ﴿We found our fathers upon an ummah﴾; i.e., upon a millah.

If someone says: these words come with several meanings, what determines the meaning?

* Students: The context.

* The Shaykh: The context and the indicators of the situation. If you say to a rich man: "Wear the cloak," and to a poor man: "Wear the cloak," do the two cloaks differ? The first, the rich man: wear a rich man's cloak; the second: wear a poor man's cloak. See, the meaning differs according to the state of the addressee. So what is important is that what determines the meaning is the context.

For this reason we said: there is no majaz (figurative usage) in the Arabic language at all, nor in the Qur'an. This question has three opinions:

The first opinion: majaz occurs in the Arabic language and in the Qur'an. This is the view of the majority of scholars.

The second: it occurs in the language but not in the Qur'an. This was chosen by a group, among them Shaykh Muhammad al-Amin al-Shinqiti, author of Adwa' al-Bayan.

And among them are those who said: there is no majaz in the Qur'an or in the language. This is the view chosen by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, and his student Ibn al-Qayyim, and this is the truth, because a word has no inherent meaning; the word is within a sentence, so when a word in a given position indicates one of its meanings, that is its literal (haqiqah) meaning. If you said: "I saw a lion carrying a bag to the mosque to read," could it occur to anyone that by "lion" is meant the well-known wild beast? No, rather if someone claimed this, everyone would refute him. What prevented this?

* Student: The context.

* The Shaykh: The context. So "lion" here is literal in its place, and it indicates bravery. Instead of saying "I saw a brave man carrying a bag," I say "I saw a lion." Pay attention to this, for it contains a great benefit.

People often argue, saying: how can there be no majaz in the Qur'an when Allah says: ﴿And they found within it a wall about to collapse (yurid an yanqadda)﴾ [al-Kahf 77]; i.e., inclining. Does the wall have no will?

We say: first, we deny your statement that the wall has no will; rather it has will without doubt. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿The seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them exalt Him. And there is not a thing except that it exalts [Allah] by His praise, but you do not understand their exaltation﴾ [al-Isra 44]. Do these creatures glorify with will or without will?

* Students: With will.

* The Shaykh: With will, without doubt; otherwise there would be no praise of Allah in it.

Second, we say: what prevents will in inanimate matter, when the Prophet ﷺ is authentically reported to have said about Uhud, which is a mountain of stone: "This is a mountain that loves us and we love it" [Agreed upon; al-Bukhari with this wording (1481), and Muslim (1392/503), from the hadith of Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi, may Allah be pleased with him]. He affirmed love for this mountain, and love is more specific than will.

Third, we say: the will of everything is according to its nature. The inclining of the wall means it wishes to fall, as a person's bowing means he wishes to bow, for example, and there is no obstacle.

They say: Fine, you have escaped this. What do you say about His saying: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾ [al-Isra 24]? The meaning: be humble to them out of mercy for them. They say: does humility have a wing? We say: humility is a non-physical matter, and when a person is not humble he becomes haughty and exalts himself. So He said "wing of humility" instead of "wing of haughtiness." The wing is mentioned because it is what birds fly with to the sky. The verse clearly means: be lowly to the two parents, humble yourself to them, and lower the wing to them; this is the utmost of humility toward them.

* Student: O Shaykh, may Allah bless you, if we say there is majaz, what is the legal prohibition in affirming majaz?

* The Shaykh: The first prohibition: majaz, by agreement of those who affirm it, can be negated, and this means the Qur'an could be denied. For instance, one says: "yurid an yanqadda" — the wall has no will. Is this valid?

* Student: It is not valid.

* The Shaykh: It is not valid. For this reason al-Shinqiti, may Allah have mercy on him, relied strongly on this argument. He said: the most prominent sign of majaz is that it can be negated, and there is nothing in the Qur'an that can be negated. That is the first.

Second: this majaz, which Ibn al-Qayyim called a taghut (idol/false authority), was used by them to reach the denial of the attributes. They said: the hand is a majaz for blessing; the istiwa' (settling) is a majaz for istila' (taking control); the eye is a majaz for encompassing; and so on.

Whoever says that Shaykh al-Islam and Ibn al-Qayyim denied this and were severe in denying it because the people of ta'til (denial of attributes) reached the denial of the attributes through majaz, this is a lie against them both, Shaykh al-Islam and Ibn al-Qayyim. Rather, they denied it absolutely, even in the simplest things.

* Student: O Shaykh, may Allah reward you, regarding the reading of Nafi': ﴿And they made the angels, who are with the Most Merciful, females﴾ [al-Zukhruf 19].

* The Shaykh: ﴿'ibad (servants)﴾, as it comes in the Qur'an.

* Student: No, in the reading of Nafi' (...)?

* The Shaykh: ﴿'Ibad al-Rahman (servants of the Most Merciful)﴾, as it comes in the Qur'an.

* Student: May Allah reward you with good, O Shaykh. What is the response to those who say that majaz in the Qur'an indicates the eloquence and inimitability of the noble Qur'an?

* The Shaykh: Wrong. How would it indicate its eloquence when it can be negated and denied?!

* Student: I say: in the book Fath Rabb al-Bariyyah, it seems to be understood from the speech that the basis of majaz is affirmed, because you said: the majazi meaning is not accepted except with three conditions. And among the arguments of those who affirm majaz, they say: the Qur'an came in the styles of the language, and the language contains majaz, meaning that among the miracles of the Qur'an is that it did not depart from the styles...

* The Shaykh: Yes, but we say: the language contains no majaz at all; that is, we deny the basis. As for what we wrote first in Usul al-Fiqh, where we mentioned majaz, we were following a plan drawn up for us by the institutes, and not out of our own conviction. We had warned them that they must write a marginal note on this, saying: this is according to the view of majaz, and that we do not hold that. I do not know whether they wrote it or not.

* * *
All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds, and may Allah's blessings and peace be upon our Prophet Muhammad, and upon his family and companions and those who follow them in goodness until the Day of Judgment.

Before we begin today's lesson, I want to draw your attention to the purpose of learning. The purpose of knowledge is to act upon what you know. Among that is adorning oneself with noble character and high manners. We have seen from you a great coarseness, greater than the coarseness of the Bedouins, and a lack of concern for Islamic manners and ethics. The least and easiest thing is spreading the greeting of peace (salam). Spreading the salam is one of the causes of entering Paradise, because of the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "By Allah, you will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I not inform you of something which, if you do it, you will love one another? Spread the salam among yourselves" [Narrated by Muslim (54/93) and Abu Dawud (5193), with this wording from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him]. This is absent in many of you. I do not know why you learn! I do not know until when you will not adorn yourselves with virtuous character! A person passes by his brothers and does not greet them with salam. Is this from the manners of Islam? Answer.

* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: Is this from the manners of a student of knowledge?

* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: Is this from the manners of a person of muruwwah (manliness and honor)?

* Students: No.

* The Shaykh: Subhan Allah! I do not know how I should sow, and then a crop comes up with no fruit in it. What is the benefit? If there is no tangible fruit, a person may be overtaken by despair and say: these people only came for theoretical knowledge without practice. And this is despite the fact that when a person greets his brother with salam, he gains ten good deeds, which will benefit him on the Day of Resurrection when he has no dirham or dinar.

Please pay attention, please have manners, please act upon what you know, otherwise there is no benefit.

I say this from my heart, and I hope it settles in your hearts. Subhan Allah! Subhan Allah! Subhan Allah! A man passes by his companion side by side and does not greet him, and no manners are apparent.

Let us set aside other things. There may also be other things that violate manliness and Islamic manners, but this is the clearest and most evident. I hope I do not find any of you adorned with this blameworthy trait, namely not spreading the salam. Greet, my brother; what harms you? Shaytan may say to him: do not greet this one, because he is standing with his companion, and there may be secret conversations between them. You greet, and if they return it, that is what is required; and if they do not return it, then if they have an excuse they are excused, and if they have no excuse, they are sinful. I hope I do not return to this matter on the basis that you have been steadfast. And Allah is the Granter of success.

* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Shaytan: ﴿He said: "Even if I brought you better guidance than what you found your fathers upon?" They said: "Indeed, we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent."﴾ [al-Zukhruf 24].
* The Shaykh: But why do you say: ﴿They said﴾ ﴿They said: indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾?

* Student: Repetition, O Shaykh.

* The Shaykh: Stop at His saying: ﴿better guidance than what you found your fathers upon﴾, stop, and do not (...) ﴿They said﴾, then return and say: ﴿They said﴾. This is a habit of many readers who claim they have perfected the recitation of the Qur'an: you find him stopping at a place other than a proper stop, then repeating the word, or perhaps the sentence. My brother, stop at the first proper stopping point, then continue. If he wanted to repeat it so that the speech flows continuously, we say: repeat the preceding sentence as well, until he completes the beginning of the verse.

Then I say: if the breath runs out, begin from where the breath ran out, absolutely, because this pause is for an excuse. Why repeat the word? Do you not know the saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿So woe to those who pray﴾ [al-Ma'un 4], a verse on which one may stop, and then begin: ﴿who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'un 5]? Stopping at verses is permitted even if the second is connected to the first, and stopping for an excuse is permitted even if the second is connected to the first; one resumes from where one stopped.

The student: "He said: 'Even if I brought you better guidance than what you found your fathers following?' They said: 'We disbelieve in what you have been sent with.' So We took vengeance on them, then see how was the end of the deniers. And when Abraham said to his father and his people: 'Indeed, I am free of what you worship, except He who created me, for He will guide me.' And he made it a word lasting among his descendants that they might return. Rather, I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers until there came to them the truth and a clear Messenger.'" [Az-Zukhruf 24–29].

The Shaykh: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "And likewise, We did not send before you any warner into a city but that its affluent ones said: 'Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps.'" [Az-Zukhruf 23]. That is, what has been said to you has been said to those before you.

"We did not send before you any warner into a city but that its affluent ones said: 'Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion'" [Az-Zukhruf 23]. The wisdom in this is to console the Prophet (ﷺ) in one respect, and to warn those who deny him in another respect, and that what befell others will befall them, since they insisted on imitating their fathers in falsehood.

And His saying: "We did not send before you any warner into a city." Read the tafsir.

Student: "And likewise, We did not send before you any warner into a city but that its affluent ones said..." i.e., those made luxurious (mutrafūhā), like the saying of your people.

The Shaykh: No, is it "mutanaʿʿimūhā" or "munaʿʿamūhā"?

Student: "Mutanaʿʿimūhā."

The Shaykh: With a tā'?

Student: Yes, in my copy it has a tā'.

The Shaykh: No, that is a mistake; "munaʿʿamūhā" (made luxurious) is the correct reading.

Student: ("Munaʿʿamūhā, like the saying of your people: 'Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion (ummah)', i.e., a creed (millah), 'and indeed we are following in their footsteps', i.e., following them.")

The Shaykh: The wisdom of this is the consolation of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the warning to these deniers: that all previous nations said to their peoples: "Indeed, we found our fathers upon a religion (ummah)", i.e., a creed (millah), "and indeed we are following in their footsteps", i.e., the religion they followed, "[are] following", i.e., adhering to and imitating.

In this noble verse there are benefits. Among them: the consolation of the Prophet (ﷺ), that what was said to him had been said to those before him, as in His saying, Exalted is He: "Nothing is said to you except what was said to the messengers before you" [Fussilat 43].

Among them: the agreement of the people of falsehood upon one aim, namely denying the messengers and following their fathers.

Among them: the prohibition of imitation (taqlid) in falsehood. As for imitation in truth, there is no harm in it. So if a man does not know the ruling on a matter in the religion of Allah and has no capacity for independent reasoning (ijtihad), his duty is taqlid, based on the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: "So ask the people of remembrance if you do not know" [An-Nahl 43], and the saying of Allah, Exalted is He: "Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity" [Al-Baqarah 286], and His saying: "So fear Allah as much as you are able" [At-Taghabun 16].

As for one who prohibits taqlid absolutely, his statement is false and contradicts the apparent meaning of the Qur'an; and as for one who obliges it absolutely, his statement is false and contradicts what must be believed regarding following the messengers.

So the correct view is that taqlid is permissible in cases of necessity. For this reason Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah said: "Taqlid is like eating carrion: if a person is compelled to it, it is permissible; otherwise, it is not."

But can we say to the layman, the marketplace man: "Strive in this matter until you know the ruling of Allah"? It is not possible; if he kept striving, he would become confused. Rather, his duty is to ask.

Is taqlid permitted in the principles of religion (usul al-din) or only in its branches (furu' al-din)?

The answer: first, the division of religion into principles and branches is a later innovation that was not known in the time of the Companions. What shows its invalidity is that they count prayer, zakat, fasting and hajj among the branches of religion, even though they are the pillars of Islam. The correct view is that the Sharia does not divide into principles and branches; this is a newly coined terminology. Rather, it divides into scholarly principles (usul 'ilmiyyah) and practical principles (usul 'amaliyyah): the scholarly principles are the beliefs, and the practical ones are the obligatory acts of worship. This is what the text indicates.

So we say: our question, "Is taqlid permitted in the principles of religion and its branches, or in its branches only?" The very division is a newly invented innovation, though most scholars now follow it, and it is also not correct. What is the proof of its invalidity?

Student: That they made prayer...

The Shaykh: That they made prayer, zakat, fasting and hajj branches of religion, while they are a principle of religion: the pillars of Islam.

Then we say: taqlid in what you call the principles and branches of religion is permissible. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed; so ask the people of remembrance if you do not know" [An-Nahl 43]. Is prophethood, by this division of theirs, among the principles or the branches?

Student: Among the principles.

The Shaykh: Prophethood is among the principles, a matter of belief. Yet Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "We did not send before you except men... so ask the people of remembrance." Ask: did We send men or angels? "If you do not know." The rule is that whoever cannot reach the truth by himself must practise taqlid, whether in matters of knowledge or practice; there is no difference.

Among the benefits of this noble verse: these deniers of the messengers have no proof except the mere practice of their fathers, and this is not a proof.

On this basis, it is not permissible to argue by the practice of people, as some folk do. If you forbid someone from something, he says: "Everyone does it." This is not a proof, and you cannot meet Allah with this argument: "Everyone does this" will not benefit you before Allah. Say instead: "The Book indicates its permissibility," or "the Sunnah indicates its permissibility." We say: yes, with all respect. But "everyone does it" is not acceptable.

Student: (﴿He said﴾, i.e., to them: ﴿Even if I brought you something better guided than what you found your fathers following?﴾ They said: ﴿Indeed, we deny that with which you have been sent﴾ — you and those before you.)

* Shaykh: ﴿He said, "Even if I brought you...﴾ — "He" refers to the Messenger whom Allah, Mighty and Majestic, sent, and who was met with their claim that they found their fathers upon a community. He said to them: ﴿Even if I brought you something better guided than what you found your fathers upon?﴾ That is: Will you reject my word and follow what your fathers were upon, even if I brought you something better than it? The interrogative here is clearly for denunciation and reproach; that is: how can you follow what your fathers were upon when I have brought you something better?

That is: Will you reject my word and follow what your fathers were upon, even if I brought you something better than it? The interrogative here is clearly for denunciation and reproach; that is: how can you follow what your fathers were upon when I have brought you something better? ﴿Even if I brought you something better guided than what you found your fathers upon﴾ [az-Zukhruf 24], namely the legislation of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Despite this, their response is the same: ﴿They said, "Indeed, we deny that with which you have been sent"﴾ [az-Zukhruf 24]. This is the utmost of obstinacy; that is, even if you bring us something better guided than what we found our fathers upon, we are still disbelievers. They do not say, as they said first, ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community﴾ [az-Zukhruf 23], but rather they say ﴿disbelievers﴾ absolutely. This is the strongest form of obstinacy — we ask Allah for well-being. This is like the saying of those who were arrogant among the people of Salih: ﴿Those who were arrogant said, "Indeed, we deny that in which you have believed"﴾ [al-A'raf 76].

* In this verse: the demonstration of how the messengers, peace be upon them, dealt with the deniers, by presenting to them persuasive proofs, but the disbelievers remain obstinate.

* Among its lessons: the permissibility of comparing two things where the other side may contain nothing of the meaning. His saying ﴿better guided﴾ is a comparative form (ism tafdil), yet we say that what they found their fathers upon contains no guidance at all. But descending to the level of the opponent is not objectionable even if the other side has nothing in it. Consider the saying of Allah, Exalted: ﴿Is Allah better, or what they associate with Him?﴾ [an-Naml 59]. These idols — is there any good in idols?

* Students: No.

* Shaykh: No. But for the sake of arguing with the opponent, we say to him: Is Allah better, or your gods? While we know that there is no good in them. Here He said: ﴿Even if I brought you something better guided than what you found your fathers upon﴾, though it is known that what their fathers were upon contains no guidance, but is rather misguidance. However, the addressee regards it as guidance, so we address him according to his level of understanding. Among this is what Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah and other scholars used in disputing with the people of kalam (Ahl al-Kalam), where they proceed in their argument on the basis of their terminology, even though they reject the fundamental basis of what they hold. Yet arguing with an opponent is not objectionable, where a person descends to the opponent's understanding, so that the argument against him becomes more forceful.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that those obstinate ones who follow what they found their fathers upon have no intention of believing, because when they were overcome in argument, what did they say? ﴿They said, "Indeed, we deny that with which you have been sent"﴾. That is: they will never believe, no matter what proof you bring. This is the utmost of arrogance toward the truth.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So We took vengeance upon them, and observe how was the end of the deniers﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 25]. "We took vengeance upon them" means: We sent down retribution upon them, and retribution is punishment. "Observe how was the end of the deniers": look, O Muhammad, or look, O listener, at how the end of the deniers was. If we look, we find that the end was destruction and annihilation, so let us take heed.

* In this noble verse: a demonstration of the power of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and that He, blessed and exalted, gives the wrongdoer respite until, when He seizes him, He does not let him escape. Allah is able to take vengeance upon them at the first instance, but He gives the wrongdoer respite; and when He seizes him, He seizes him with the seizing of the Mighty, the Powerful.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the command to take heed and to reflect upon matters, based on His saying: ﴿observe how was the end of the deniers﴾. Is the "looking" here a looking of the eye or a looking of the heart?

* The students: The heart.

* The Shaykh: A looking of the heart.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the end of the deniers is destruction and annihilation, because Allah destroyed all the deniers. He destroyed the people of Nuh, the people of Hud, the people of Salih, the people of Lut, and Pharaoh. Allah the Mighty and Majestic destroyed all the deniers. But this Ummah, praise be to Allah, has had Allah make the destruction of its enemy at its own hands, through warfare; for the destruction of your enemy at your hand is more healing to you than his destruction at the hand of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. It is more healing for the heart. Is it not so?

* The students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: Yes, we say: yes. The destruction of your enemy at your hand is more healing for you than his destruction at the hand of Allah the Mighty and Majestic. This is why the destruction of those who denied the Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) came at the hands of the believers, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands and will disgrace them and give you victory over them and heal the breasts of a believing people. And He will remove the rage of their hearts﴾ [At-Tawbah: 14-15].

* Also among the benefits of this noble verse: the obligation of reflection and taking heed.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the end of those who deny the messengers is destruction and annihilation.

* Among its benefits: a warning to this Ummah against denying its Messenger, lest there befall them what befell others.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verses 26–28 (part 1 of 2):**

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free from what you worship"﴾ [az-Zukhruf 26]. The word *idh* (إذ) is an object (*maf'ul*) governing an omitted verb (*muqaddar*), and the estimated sense is: "Remember when Abraham said." Abraham is mentioned because all the nations claim descent from him. The Jews said he was a Jew, the Christians said he was a Christian, and the Arabs said they follow his religion (*millah*). Allah wished to show that Abraham, peace be upon him, was free of *shirk* (association of others with Allah) and of its people. ﴿And when Abraham said﴾: *idh* is what?

* Student: *Idh* is a verb that explains the omitted element.
* Shaykh: A verb, or a subject, or an object?
* Student: The estimated word is: "Remember."
* Shaykh: Yes, but what is its grammatical analysis (*i'rab*)?
* Student: The omitted element is estimated as "Remember."
* Shaykh: Well done. Its estimate is: "Remember this event, when Abraham said." ﴿When he said﴾: remember when Abraham said. Abraham the Friend of Allah, peace be upon him, is the leader of the *hunafa'* (people of pure monotheism), concerning whom Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Then We revealed to you, "Follow the religion of Abraham, a man of pure faith (*hanif*), and he was not among the polytheists"﴾ [an-Nahl 123]. ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free from what you worship"﴾. ﴿To his father﴾ is Azar. ﴿And his people﴾ are those to whom he was sent. Allah, blessed and exalted, has mentioned Abraham's argument with his father in detail in surah Maryam, and in other places in brief or in moderate detail.

The dialogue between him and his father took place in surah Maryam, where Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And mention in the Book Abraham. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet. When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees and does not benefit you at all?"﴾ [Maryam 41–42]. If you call upon it, it does not hear you; if you agree with it, it does not see you; if you seek its help, it does not benefit you, and it does not avail you at all. What comes next?

* Student: ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾ [Maryam 43].
* Shaykh: ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾. The address here is built on gentleness, softness, and humility before the father. ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾. He did not say, "O my father, you are ignorant and I am knowledgeable." Rather, he said: ﴿Indeed, there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾. This is from his good manners, peace be upon him. What came to him was revelation, and his father did not have it. What came to him was the knowledge of monotheism, and his father did not have it. ﴿So follow me﴾: the son says to his father, "Follow me," because the son has the truth and the father does not.
﴿I will guide you to a straight path﴾ [Maryam 43]. ﴿O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has been, to the Most Merciful, disobedient﴾ [Maryam 44]. ﴿Do not worship Satan﴾ means the worship of obedience. Whoever obeys something has worshipped it, according to the circumstances. ﴿Indeed, Satan has been disobedient﴾ means "disobedient." ﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would become a companion to Satan﴾ [Maryam 45]: that is, it will befall you. He made being a companion of Satan a form of punishment, because a person turning away from the truth is itself a calamity resulting from some sins, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And if they turn away, then know that Allah only wants to afflict them for some of their sins﴾ [al-Ma'idah 49]. Stop here. We tend to think that punishments are only the trials that befall a person, such as illness, poverty, loss of loved ones, and similar things. This is true, yes, these are punishments, but there is a greater punishment, which is ... ﴿And if they turn away, then know that Allah only wants to afflict them for some of their sins﴾. This is greater than the punishment of a physical, bodily trial. For this reason he said: ﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would become a companion to Satan﴾ [Maryam 45]. What was the father's reply? The father's reply was harsh: ﴿He said, "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?"﴾ [Maryam 46]. Look, he denied him his desire. This is why the scholars of rhetoric (*balaghah*) said that the word which comes right after the interrogative particle *hamzah* (همزة الاستفهام) is the element being denied. He did not say, "O Abraham, do you turn away?" Rather, he began with the denial, in the manner of ... ﴿Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?﴾. This is an interrogative of denial and rebuke. ﴿If you do not cease﴾ [Maryam 46], meaning: from your calling me to monotheism. ﴿If you do not cease﴾, what?

* Students: ﴿I will surely stone you﴾ [Maryam 46].
* Shaykh: ﴿I will surely stone you.﴾ It is a threat that the father makes to his son, while the son softens toward him and pleads with him, saying, "O father, O father, O father." Here is the father's reply. This statement, ﴿If you do not cease, I will surely stone you﴾, was also said by others who denied the messengers. Pharaoh said to Moses: ﴿I will surely make you one of the imprisoned﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 29].
﴿And leave me for a long time﴾ [Maryam 46]: that is, abandon me. ﴿For a long time﴾ means a long period. He means: leave me as I am and do not speak to me.
﴿He said, "Peace be upon you"﴾ [Maryam 47]. This is Abraham's final word. How forbearing he was, peace be upon him. This is why Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing﴾ [at-Tawbah 114]. ﴿He said, "Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He has always been gracious to me"﴾ [Maryam 47]. He asked forgiveness for him until Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, forbade him.

The point of all this is that Abraham's father was a polytheist, is that not so?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: What is his name?
* Students: Azar.
* Shaykh: Azar, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods?"﴾ [al-An'am 74]. It is strange that some people, may Allah protect us, have distorted the words of Allah away from what He intended, following their own desires. They say: "Abraham's father was not a polytheist; rather he was upon monotheism. It is impossible for the father of a Prophet to be a polytheist. Azar was his paternal uncle, not his father." La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah (there is no might or power except with Allah). See how desire works! "Whoever speaks about the Quran according to his own opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire"[[Narrated by at-Tirmidhi (2951) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]. How can one say, "He was not his father but his uncle," when the Quran says: ﴿When Abraham said to his father Azar﴾? How can one say he was his uncle when he says: ﴿O my father﴾? Is the one who says this not ashamed? Does he not fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by altering the words from their places, based on a corrupt belief that the father of a Messenger cannot be a disbeliever? We say: Glory be to Allah! Consider this: that the father of the Messenger was a disbeliever while his son was a great Prophet is the greatest evidence of Allah's power, and that He brings the living out of the dead, and that lineage does not elevate its owners. Is that not so, O people?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: By Allah, if we said this to an elderly woman among the elderly Muslims, that Azar was Abraham's paternal uncle and not his father, she would criticise us. Rather, we say: Abraham's father was a disbeliever, and Muhammad's father was a disbeliever, and what harm does it do to the Prophet that his father was a disbeliever? It harms him in no way. Rather, this is the greatest proof of the perfection of Allah's power, that He brings Prophets out from the loins of these disbelievers. But praise be to Allah, no Prophet has ever come from an illicit union, never. As for the matter of disbelief and faith, this does not count as an affront to the honour of the Prophets.

The point of all this is that Abraham, peace be upon him, openly told his father and his people: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾ [az-Zukhruf 26]. ﴿Free﴾: the mufassir (commentator) said "*bari'*" (بريء), and this is a shortcoming on the part of the mufassir, because *bara'* (براء) is a *sifah mushabbahah* (an adjective-like form, a stable quality), while *bari'* (بريء) is an *ism al-fa'il* (active participle). Which is greater? The *sifah mushabbahah* is greater, because it indicates permanence, stability, and continuity. So *bara'* is greater than *bari'*. ﴿Bara'﴾ means the quality of freedom: a permanent, fixed, continuous disassociation from what you are upon. ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who created me﴾ [az-Zukhruf 26–27]. I think it is not possible to complete the verse; time has run out.

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿And He made it a lasting word among his descendants that they might return. Rather, I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger. But when the truth came to them, they said, "This is magic, and indeed we are disbelievers in it"﴾ [az-Zukhruf 28–30].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And He made it a lasting word among his descendants that they might return.﴾
* Student: The verse before it.
* Shaykh: The one before it? ﴿And when Abraham said﴾?
* Student: The one after it.
* Shaykh: This is ﴿And He made it a lasting word﴾.
* Student: ﴿Except He who created me, for He will guide me﴾.
* Shaykh: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free from what you worship"﴾. Here, *idh* (إذ), what is its position in grammatical analysis?
* Student: Object.
* Shaykh: Why?
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: The estimate is: "Remember when he said." Yes, remember, meaning to these deniers: remember this statement that Abraham, peace be upon him, made, the one they took pride in claiming descent from and following his religion, so that the proof may be established against them. ﴿When he said﴾. ﴿To his father and his people﴾: his father is Azar, and he had debates with him that were discussed earlier. ﴿And his people﴾ are the ones he was sent to. Abraham, peace be upon him, like the other Prophets, was sent specifically to his own people, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have been given five things that none of the Prophets before me were given," among them: "A Prophet used to be sent only to his own people, but I have been sent to all mankind"[[Agreed upon (Muttafaq 'alayh); al-Bukhari (438) and Muslim (521/3) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them both.]].

﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾. This sentence is emphasised, as is well known, by *inna* (إنّ), and *bara'* (براء) is a *sifah mushabbahah*, which is more eloquent than the word *bari'* (بريء), because the *sifah mushabbahah* implies permanence and stability. ﴿From what you worship﴾: that is, from that which you worship. ﴿Except He who created me﴾. What is meant by "you worship" is the idols they carved with their own hands and then worshipped. This is why Abraham, peace be upon him, said to them in one of his debates: ﴿He said, "Do you worship what you carve, when Allah created you and what you make?"﴾ [as-Saffat 95–96]. How can you worship them when they are created? How can you worship them when you are the ones who carve them? As for His saying ﴿Except He who created me﴾: *illa* (إلا) is the particle of exception. But is the exception here disconnected (*munqati'*) or connected (*muttasil*)? The answer: if they worshipped Allah and other than Him, the exception is connected; if they did not worship Allah, the exception is disconnected. A disconnected exception is one where what follows *illa* is not of the same kind as what precedes it. The grammarians illustrated this with their saying: "The people came except a donkey." Is the donkey of the same kind as the people, or of a different kind?

* Student: Of a different kind.
* Shaykh: Of a different kind, so the exception is disconnected. But if it is said: "The people came except Zayd," the exception here is connected, because Zayd is of the same kind as the one excepted from. So here we apply this rule: ﴿Except He who created me﴾. If they worshipped Allah and other than Him, is the exception...?
* Students: Connected.
* Shaykh: Connected. And if they did not worship Allah, the exception is disconnected. As for His saying ﴿Except He who created me﴾, He did not say "Except Allah," in order to establish the proof that none deserves worship except Him. The One who originated you the first time and brought you into existence from nothing is the One who deserves to be worshipped, because He is the Creator of you. Pay attention.

That is to say, if someone asks: "Why did He not say, 'Except Allah'?" The answer: to establish the proof that none should be worshipped except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is like His saying: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you﴾ [al-Baqarah 21]. It is well known that *Rabb* (رب, Lord) means Creator, yet He said ﴿who created you﴾, though this is already known, in order to establish the proof that He alone deserves worship. ﴿Except He who created me﴾: the author said, "who created me."

﴿For He will guide me﴾: He will guide me to His religion. Guidance is of two kinds, as will be explained, if Allah wills, in the statement of benefits. ﴿And He made it﴾: that is, the word of monotheism understood from His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [as-Saffat 99]. ﴿He made it﴾: the pronoun refers to the word he spoke. What was the word he spoke? Listen to the words of the mufassir: he said it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾. This is an error on the part of the author. The word he spoke is the nearest word, which is: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship (26), except He who created me﴾, and it is the word of monotheism. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord, He will guide me﴾, it has no connection to this verse. So ﴿He made it﴾: the pronoun refers to what?

* Student: His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free﴾.
* Shaykh: No. ﴿He made it﴾: the pronoun refers to what? To the word he spoke, which is?
* Student: ﴿Indeed, I am free﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship (26), except He who created me﴾. The meaning of His saying ﴿He made it﴾ is: He appointed it as the path that those after him would follow. ﴿A lasting word among his descendants﴾: among whose descendants?

* Student: The descendants of Abraham.
* Shaykh: The descendants of Abraham. He said: that is, his offspring. So there will always be among them someone who affirms the oneness of Allah. This is what the author said: that the meaning is that this word will remain among his descendants, and that the whole progeny cannot associate others with Allah, but that some must remain. The correct view is different from this. The correct meaning is: He made this word the only word that those after him would follow, whether they adhered to it or not.

﴿That they might return﴾: that is, the people of Makkah. If it were said that ﴿that they might return﴾ refers to his descendants, that would be a more general meaning than what the author said, since the verses do not mention the people of Makkah but mention "descendants." It is well known that the people of Makkah are of his descendants, and that the Children of Israel are of his descendants. If we say that the pronoun in ﴿that they might return﴾ refers to ﴿his descendants﴾, it becomes more general than what the author said, because the author limited it to a part of the descendants, and this is clearly a deficiency. For this reason, adopt this principle: do not interpret the Quran in a more restricted sense than what it indicates. In other words, if the Quran indicates something general, do not restrict it unless there is evidence; otherwise leave it in its generality. So ﴿And He made it a lasting word among his descendants that they might return﴾ [az-Zukhruf 28]: the pronoun refers to whom?

* Students: His descendants.
* Shaykh: To the descendants: from Quraysh and the Children of Israel. But what is the meaning of ﴿He made it a lasting word﴾? According to the author, may Allah have mercy on him, the mufassir means that this word will remain among the descendants, so monotheism can never be lost from them. The correct view is that He made it a legislated appointment (*ja'lan shar'iyyan*), meaning that He charged his descendants to worship Allah alone, the Mighty and Majestic. Some of them obeyed, and some of them disobeyed.

* In this noble verse there is a great virtue of Abraham, peace be upon him, which is his declaration of freedom from what his people worshipped: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verses 26–28 (part 2 of 2):**

* Among its lessons: pure monotheism (tawhid) in Ibrahim, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who created me﴾. This is the meaning of the words "there is no god but Allah" (la ilaha illa Allah). So "Indeed, I am free" corresponds to "there is no god" (la ilaha), and "except He who created me" corresponds to "but Allah" (illa Allah). Answer me!
* Students: "But Allah" (illa Allah).
* Shaykh: It corresponds to "but Allah." So this statement, ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾, has exactly the meaning of "there is no god but Allah." Is that not so?
* Student: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person should support a ruling with evidence (dalil), because that is more eloquent. This is shown when Ibrahim said: ﴿except He who created me﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: strength of hope, meaning Ibrahim's hope in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, based on his saying: ﴿for indeed He will guide me﴾. The "sin" here (in sa-yahdeni) indicates certainty. Guidance (hidayah) is of two kinds. The first kind is guidance by indication (hidayat al-dalala, the guidance of showing the way), which comes from Allah and from the servants of Allah. The second is guidance to the truth through divine enabling (hidayat al-tawfiq), which comes only from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; no one possesses it. Listen: guidance is of two kinds. The first?
* Students: Guidance by indication.
* Shaykh: Guidance by indication, meaning pointing to the truth. This comes from Allah and from others. The second is guidance of enabling, which comes only from Allah alone; no one possesses it. We ask Allah to guide us and you.

Then, the verses that mention guidance are of three types: some must be understood as guidance of enabling, some must be understood as guidance of indication, and some include both. Take the words of the worshipper in prayer: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatiha 6]. Does it include…?

* Students: Guidance by indication.
* Shaykh: Both: guidance by indication, which is knowledge, and guidance of enabling, which is action. So, O worshipper, do you feel this when you say: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾? Or do you feel that you are only reciting a Qur'an? Tell us honestly.
* Student: The second.
* Shaykh: Usually the second. Not all people, but most people say ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ reading it as a verse to be recited. They do not feel that the meaning is: guide me, teach me, and enable me to act. They do not feel this. But feel this, so that you know what you are saying "amen" to.

An example of guidance by indication alone is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura 52]. What kind of guidance is this?

* Students: Indication.
* Shaykh: Indication, meaning you point people to the straight path. An example of guidance of enabling is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾ [al-Qasas 56]. He says this to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: you cannot grant anyone guidance, even if you love them. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) tried, when his uncle Abu Talib was present in his final moments, to make him profess Allah's oneness, but he was unable. He said at the time of death: "O uncle, say: there is no god but Allah, a word by which I can argue for you before Allah."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3884) from the hadith of al-Musayyib ibn Hazn, may Allah be pleased with him.]] Two men of Quraysh who were bad companions were with him, and they said to Abu Talib: "Will you turn away from the religion of Abd al-Muttalib?" See, may Allah protect us, the pride! "Will you turn away from the religion of Abd al-Muttalib?" meaning his grandfather, whom Quraysh took pride in. So the last thing he said was: "He is on the religion of Abd al-Muttalib," and he refused to say: "There is no god but Allah."

So what guidance was the Prophet (ﷺ) unable to give in this case?

* Students: Guidance of enabling.
* Shaykh: Guidance of enabling. As for guidance of indication, he said: "Say: there is no god but Allah."

The saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat 17]. Which of the two kinds is this?

* Students: Indication.
* Shaykh: Guidance of indication. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He chose him and guided him to a straight path﴾ [al-Nahl 121].

* Students: It includes both.
* Shaykh: It includes both together.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the complete sincere advice of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to his descendants (aqib), since he made the word of tawhid remain among them. This is like a bequest to his descendants that they should carry out this bequest.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: returning to the truth that the forefathers held, based on His saying: ﴿so that they may return﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verses 26–28 (part 1 of 2):**

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free from what you worship"﴾ [az-Zukhruf 26]. The word *idh* (إذ) is an object (*maf'ul*) governing an omitted verb (*muqaddar*), and the estimated sense is: "Remember when Abraham said."
