Abraham is mentioned because all the nations claim descent from him. The Jews said he was a Jew, the Christians said he was a Christian, and the Arabs said they follow his religion (*millah*). Allah wished to show that Abraham, peace be upon him, was free of *shirk* (association of others with Allah) and of its people. ﴿And when Abraham said﴾: *idh* is what?

* Student: *Idh* is a verb that explains the omitted element.
* Shaykh: A verb, or a subject, or an object?
* Student: The estimated word is: "Remember."
* Shaykh: Yes, but what is its grammatical analysis (*i'rab*)?
* Student: The omitted element is estimated as "Remember."
* Shaykh: Well done. Its estimate is: "Remember this event, when Abraham said." ﴿When he said﴾: remember when Abraham said. Abraham the Friend of Allah, peace be upon him, is the leader of the *hunafa'* (people of pure monotheism), concerning whom Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Then We revealed to you, "Follow the religion of Abraham, a man of pure faith (*hanif*), and he was not among the polytheists"﴾ [an-Nahl 123]. ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free from what you worship"﴾. ﴿To his father﴾ is Azar. ﴿And his people﴾ are those to whom he was sent. Allah, blessed and exalted, has mentioned Abraham's argument with his father in detail in surah Maryam, and in other places in brief or in moderate detail.

The dialogue between him and his father took place in surah Maryam, where Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And mention in the Book Abraham. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet. When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees and does not benefit you at all?"﴾ [Maryam 41–42]. If you call upon it, it does not hear you; if you agree with it, it does not see you; if you seek its help, it does not benefit you, and it does not avail you at all. What comes next?

* Student: ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾ [Maryam 43].
* Shaykh: ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾. The address here is built on gentleness, softness, and humility before the father. ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾. He did not say, "O my father, you are ignorant and I am knowledgeable." Rather, he said: ﴿Indeed, there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾. This is from his good manners, peace be upon him. What came to him was revelation, and his father did not have it. What came to him was the knowledge of monotheism, and his father did not have it. ﴿So follow me﴾: the son says to his father, "Follow me," because the son has the truth and the father does not.
﴿I will guide you to a straight path﴾ [Maryam 43]. ﴿O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has been, to the Most Merciful, disobedient﴾ [Maryam 44]. ﴿Do not worship Satan﴾ means the worship of obedience. Whoever obeys something has worshipped it, according to the circumstances. ﴿Indeed, Satan has been disobedient﴾ means "disobedient." ﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would become a companion to Satan﴾ [Maryam 45]: that is, it will befall you. He made being a companion of Satan a form of punishment, because a person turning away from the truth is itself a calamity resulting from some sins, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And if they turn away, then know that Allah only wants to afflict them for some of their sins﴾ [al-Ma'idah 49]. Stop here. We tend to think that punishments are only the trials that befall a person, such as illness, poverty, loss of loved ones, and similar things. This is true, yes, these are punishments, but there is a greater punishment, which is ... ﴿And if they turn away, then know that Allah only wants to afflict them for some of their sins﴾. This is greater than the punishment of a physical, bodily trial. For this reason he said: ﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would become a companion to Satan﴾ [Maryam 45]. What was the father's reply? The father's reply was harsh: ﴿He said, "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?"﴾ [Maryam 46]. Look, he denied him his desire. This is why the scholars of rhetoric (*balaghah*) said that the word which comes right after the interrogative particle *hamzah* (همزة الاستفهام) is the element being denied. He did not say, "O Abraham, do you turn away?" Rather, he began with the denial, in the manner of ... ﴿Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?﴾. This is an interrogative of denial and rebuke. ﴿If you do not cease﴾ [Maryam 46], meaning: from your calling me to monotheism. ﴿If you do not cease﴾, what?

* Students: ﴿I will surely stone you﴾ [Maryam 46].
* Shaykh: ﴿I will surely stone you.﴾ It is a threat that the father makes to his son, while the son softens toward him and pleads with him, saying, "O father, O father, O father." Here is the father's reply. This statement, ﴿If you do not cease, I will surely stone you﴾, was also said by others who denied the messengers. Pharaoh said to Moses: ﴿I will surely make you one of the imprisoned﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 29].
﴿And leave me for a long time﴾ [Maryam 46]: that is, abandon me. ﴿For a long time﴾ means a long period. He means: leave me as I am and do not speak to me.
﴿He said, "Peace be upon you"﴾ [Maryam 47]. This is Abraham's final word. How forbearing he was, peace be upon him. This is why Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing﴾ [at-Tawbah 114]. ﴿He said, "Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He has always been gracious to me"﴾ [Maryam 47]. He asked forgiveness for him until Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, forbade him.

The point of all this is that Abraham's father was a polytheist, is that not so?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: What is his name?
* Students: Azar.
* Shaykh: Azar, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods?"﴾ [al-An'am 74]. It is strange that some people, may Allah protect us, have distorted the words of Allah away from what He intended, following their own desires. They say: "Abraham's father was not a polytheist; rather he was upon monotheism. It is impossible for the father of a Prophet to be a polytheist. Azar was his paternal uncle, not his father." La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah (there is no might or power except with Allah). See how desire works! "Whoever speaks about the Quran according to his own opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire"[[Narrated by at-Tirmidhi (2951) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]. How can one say, "He was not his father but his uncle," when the Quran says: ﴿When Abraham said to his father Azar﴾? How can one say he was his uncle when he says: ﴿O my father﴾? Is the one who says this not ashamed? Does he not fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by altering the words from their places, based on a corrupt belief that the father of a Messenger cannot be a disbeliever? We say: Glory be to Allah! Consider this: that the father of the Messenger was a disbeliever while his son was a great Prophet is the greatest evidence of Allah's power, and that He brings the living out of the dead, and that lineage does not elevate its owners. Is that not so, O people?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: By Allah, if we said this to an elderly woman among the elderly Muslims, that Azar was Abraham's paternal uncle and not his father, she would criticise us. Rather, we say: Abraham's father was a disbeliever, and Muhammad's father was a disbeliever, and what harm does it do to the Prophet that his father was a disbeliever? It harms him in no way. Rather, this is the greatest proof of the perfection of Allah's power, that He brings Prophets out from the loins of these disbelievers. But praise be to Allah, no Prophet has ever come from an illicit union, never. As for the matter of disbelief and faith, this does not count as an affront to the honour of the Prophets.

The point of all this is that Abraham, peace be upon him, openly told his father and his people: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾ [az-Zukhruf 26]. ﴿Free﴾: the mufassir (commentator) said "*bari'*" (بريء), and this is a shortcoming on the part of the mufassir, because *bara'* (براء) is a *sifah mushabbahah* (an adjective-like form, a stable quality), while *bari'* (بريء) is an *ism al-fa'il* (active participle). Which is greater? The *sifah mushabbahah* is greater, because it indicates permanence, stability, and continuity. So *bara'* is greater than *bari'*. ﴿Bara'﴾ means the quality of freedom: a permanent, fixed, continuous disassociation from what you are upon. ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who created me﴾ [az-Zukhruf 26–27]. I think it is not possible to complete the verse; time has run out.

* * *

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿And He made it a lasting word among his descendants that they might return. Rather, I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger. But when the truth came to them, they said, "This is magic, and indeed we are disbelievers in it"﴾ [az-Zukhruf 28–30].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And He made it a lasting word among his descendants that they might return.﴾
* Student: The verse before it.
* Shaykh: The one before it? ﴿And when Abraham said﴾?
* Student: The one after it.
* Shaykh: This is ﴿And He made it a lasting word﴾.
* Student: ﴿Except He who created me, for He will guide me﴾.
* Shaykh: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free from what you worship"﴾. Here, *idh* (إذ), what is its position in grammatical analysis?
* Student: Object.
* Shaykh: Why?
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: The estimate is: "Remember when he said." Yes, remember, meaning to these deniers: remember this statement that Abraham, peace be upon him, made, the one they took pride in claiming descent from and following his religion, so that the proof may be established against them. ﴿When he said﴾. ﴿To his father and his people﴾: his father is Azar, and he had debates with him that were discussed earlier. ﴿And his people﴾ are the ones he was sent to. Abraham, peace be upon him, like the other Prophets, was sent specifically to his own people, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have been given five things that none of the Prophets before me were given," among them: "A Prophet used to be sent only to his own people, but I have been sent to all mankind"[[Agreed upon (Muttafaq 'alayh); al-Bukhari (438) and Muslim (521/3) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them both.]].

﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾. This sentence is emphasised, as is well known, by *inna* (إنّ), and *bara'* (براء) is a *sifah mushabbahah*, which is more eloquent than the word *bari'* (بريء), because the *sifah mushabbahah* implies permanence and stability. ﴿From what you worship﴾: that is, from that which you worship. ﴿Except He who created me﴾. What is meant by "you worship" is the idols they carved with their own hands and then worshipped. This is why Abraham, peace be upon him, said to them in one of his debates: ﴿He said, "Do you worship what you carve, when Allah created you and what you make?"﴾ [as-Saffat 95–96]. How can you worship them when they are created? How can you worship them when you are the ones who carve them? As for His saying ﴿Except He who created me﴾: *illa* (إلا) is the particle of exception. But is the exception here disconnected (*munqati'*) or connected (*muttasil*)? The answer: if they worshipped Allah and other than Him, the exception is connected; if they did not worship Allah, the exception is disconnected. A disconnected exception is one where what follows *illa* is not of the same kind as what precedes it. The grammarians illustrated this with their saying: "The people came except a donkey." Is the donkey of the same kind as the people, or of a different kind?

* Student: Of a different kind.
* Shaykh: Of a different kind, so the exception is disconnected. But if it is said: "The people came except Zayd," the exception here is connected, because Zayd is of the same kind as the one excepted from. So here we apply this rule: ﴿Except He who created me﴾. If they worshipped Allah and other than Him, is the exception...?
* Students: Connected.
* Shaykh: Connected. And if they did not worship Allah, the exception is disconnected. As for His saying ﴿Except He who created me﴾, He did not say "Except Allah," in order to establish the proof that none deserves worship except Him. The One who originated you the first time and brought you into existence from nothing is the One who deserves to be worshipped, because He is the Creator of you. Pay attention.

That is to say, if someone asks: "Why did He not say, 'Except Allah'?" The answer: to establish the proof that none should be worshipped except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is like His saying: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you﴾ [al-Baqarah 21]. It is well known that *Rabb* (رب, Lord) means Creator, yet He said ﴿who created you﴾, though this is already known, in order to establish the proof that He alone deserves worship. ﴿Except He who created me﴾: the author said, "who created me."

﴿For He will guide me﴾: He will guide me to His religion. Guidance is of two kinds, as will be explained, if Allah wills, in the statement of benefits. ﴿And He made it﴾: that is, the word of monotheism understood from His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [as-Saffat 99]. ﴿He made it﴾: the pronoun refers to the word he spoke. What was the word he spoke? Listen to the words of the mufassir: he said it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾. This is an error on the part of the author. The word he spoke is the nearest word, which is: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship (26), except He who created me﴾, and it is the word of monotheism. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord, He will guide me﴾, it has no connection to this verse. So ﴿He made it﴾: the pronoun refers to what?

* Student: His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free﴾.
* Shaykh: No. ﴿He made it﴾: the pronoun refers to what? To the word he spoke, which is?
* Student: ﴿Indeed, I am free﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship (26), except He who created me﴾. The meaning of His saying ﴿He made it﴾ is: He appointed it as the path that those after him would follow. ﴿A lasting word among his descendants﴾: among whose descendants?

* Student: The descendants of Abraham.
* Shaykh: The descendants of Abraham. He said: that is, his offspring. So there will always be among them someone who affirms the oneness of Allah. This is what the author said: that the meaning is that this word will remain among his descendants, and that the whole progeny cannot associate others with Allah, but that some must remain. The correct view is different from this. The correct meaning is: He made this word the only word that those after him would follow, whether they adhered to it or not.

﴿That they might return﴾: that is, the people of Makkah. If it were said that ﴿that they might return﴾ refers to his descendants, that would be a more general meaning than what the author said, since the verses do not mention the people of Makkah but mention "descendants." It is well known that the people of Makkah are of his descendants, and that the Children of Israel are of his descendants. If we say that the pronoun in ﴿that they might return﴾ refers to ﴿his descendants﴾, it becomes more general than what the author said, because the author limited it to a part of the descendants, and this is clearly a deficiency. For this reason, adopt this principle: do not interpret the Quran in a more restricted sense than what it indicates. In other words, if the Quran indicates something general, do not restrict it unless there is evidence; otherwise leave it in its generality. So ﴿And He made it a lasting word among his descendants that they might return﴾ [az-Zukhruf 28]: the pronoun refers to whom?

* Students: His descendants.
* Shaykh: To the descendants: from Quraysh and the Children of Israel. But what is the meaning of ﴿He made it a lasting word﴾? According to the author, may Allah have mercy on him, the mufassir means that this word will remain among the descendants, so monotheism can never be lost from them. The correct view is that He made it a legislated appointment (*ja'lan shar'iyyan*), meaning that He charged his descendants to worship Allah alone, the Mighty and Majestic. Some of them obeyed, and some of them disobeyed.

* In this noble verse there is a great virtue of Abraham, peace be upon him, which is his declaration of freedom from what his people worshipped: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verses 26–28 (part 2 of 2):**

* Among its lessons: pure monotheism (tawhid) in Ibrahim, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who created me﴾. This is the meaning of the words "there is no god but Allah" (la ilaha illa Allah). So "Indeed, I am free" corresponds to "there is no god" (la ilaha), and "except He who created me" corresponds to "but Allah" (illa Allah). Answer me!
* Students: "But Allah" (illa Allah).
* Shaykh: It corresponds to "but Allah." So this statement, ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾, has exactly the meaning of "there is no god but Allah." Is that not so?
* Student: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person should support a ruling with evidence (dalil), because that is more eloquent. This is shown when Ibrahim said: ﴿except He who created me﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: strength of hope, meaning Ibrahim's hope in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, based on his saying: ﴿for indeed He will guide me﴾. The "sin" here (in sa-yahdeni) indicates certainty. Guidance (hidayah) is of two kinds. The first kind is guidance by indication (hidayat al-dalala, the guidance of showing the way), which comes from Allah and from the servants of Allah. The second is guidance to the truth through divine enabling (hidayat al-tawfiq), which comes only from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; no one possesses it. Listen: guidance is of two kinds. The first?
* Students: Guidance by indication.
* Shaykh: Guidance by indication, meaning pointing to the truth. This comes from Allah and from others. The second is guidance of enabling, which comes only from Allah alone; no one possesses it. We ask Allah to guide us and you.

Then, the verses that mention guidance are of three types: some must be understood as guidance of enabling, some must be understood as guidance of indication, and some include both. Take the words of the worshipper in prayer: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatiha 6]. Does it include…?

* Students: Guidance by indication.
* Shaykh: Both: guidance by indication, which is knowledge, and guidance of enabling, which is action. So, O worshipper, do you feel this when you say: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾? Or do you feel that you are only reciting a Qur'an? Tell us honestly.
* Student: The second.
* Shaykh: Usually the second. Not all people, but most people say ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ reading it as a verse to be recited. They do not feel that the meaning is: guide me, teach me, and enable me to act. They do not feel this. But feel this, so that you know what you are saying "amen" to.

An example of guidance by indication alone is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura 52]. What kind of guidance is this?

* Students: Indication.
* Shaykh: Indication, meaning you point people to the straight path. An example of guidance of enabling is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾ [al-Qasas 56]. He says this to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: you cannot grant anyone guidance, even if you love them. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) tried, when his uncle Abu Talib was present in his final moments, to make him profess Allah's oneness, but he was unable. He said at the time of death: "O uncle, say: there is no god but Allah, a word by which I can argue for you before Allah."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3884) from the hadith of al-Musayyib ibn Hazn, may Allah be pleased with him.]] Two men of Quraysh who were bad companions were with him, and they said to Abu Talib: "Will you turn away from the religion of Abd al-Muttalib?" See, may Allah protect us, the pride! "Will you turn away from the religion of Abd al-Muttalib?" meaning his grandfather, whom Quraysh took pride in. So the last thing he said was: "He is on the religion of Abd al-Muttalib," and he refused to say: "There is no god but Allah."

So what guidance was the Prophet (ﷺ) unable to give in this case?

* Students: Guidance of enabling.
* Shaykh: Guidance of enabling. As for guidance of indication, he said: "Say: there is no god but Allah."

The saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat 17]. Which of the two kinds is this?

* Students: Indication.
* Shaykh: Guidance of indication. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He chose him and guided him to a straight path﴾ [al-Nahl 121].

* Students: It includes both.
* Shaykh: It includes both together.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the complete sincere advice of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to his descendants (aqib), since he made the word of tawhid remain among them. This is like a bequest to his descendants that they should carry out this bequest.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: returning to the truth that the forefathers held, based on His saying: ﴿so that they may return﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verses 26–28 (part 1 of 2):**

Then the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free from what you worship"﴾ [az-Zukhruf 26]. The word *idh* (إذ) is an object (*maf'ul*) governing an omitted verb (*muqaddar*), and the estimated sense is: "Remember when Abraham said." Abraham is mentioned because all the nations claim descent from him. The Jews said he was a Jew, the Christians said he was a Christian, and the Arabs said they follow his religion (*millah*). Allah wished to show that Abraham, peace be upon him, was free of *shirk* (association of others with Allah) and of its people. ﴿And when Abraham said﴾: *idh* is what?

* Student: *Idh* is a verb that explains the omitted element.
* Shaykh: A verb, or a subject, or an object?
* Student: The estimated word is: "Remember."
* Shaykh: Yes, but what is its grammatical analysis (*i'rab*)?
* Student: The omitted element is estimated as "Remember."
* Shaykh: Well done. Its estimate is: "Remember this event, when Abraham said." ﴿When he said﴾: remember when Abraham said. Abraham the Friend of Allah, peace be upon him, is the leader of the *hunafa'* (people of pure monotheism), concerning whom Allah the Exalted said to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿Then We revealed to you, "Follow the religion of Abraham, a man of pure faith (*hanif*), and he was not among the polytheists"﴾ [an-Nahl 123]. ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free from what you worship"﴾. ﴿To his father﴾ is Azar. ﴿And his people﴾ are those to whom he was sent. Allah, blessed and exalted, has mentioned Abraham's argument with his father in detail in surah Maryam, and in other places in brief or in moderate detail.

The dialogue between him and his father took place in surah Maryam, where Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And mention in the Book Abraham. Indeed, he was a man of truth and a prophet. When he said to his father, "O my father, why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees and does not benefit you at all?"﴾ [Maryam 41–42]. If you call upon it, it does not hear you; if you agree with it, it does not see you; if you seek its help, it does not benefit you, and it does not avail you at all. What comes next?

* Student: ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾ [Maryam 43].
* Shaykh: ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾. The address here is built on gentleness, softness, and humility before the father. ﴿O my father, indeed there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾. He did not say, "O my father, you are ignorant and I am knowledgeable." Rather, he said: ﴿Indeed, there has come to me of knowledge that which has not come to you﴾. This is from his good manners, peace be upon him. What came to him was revelation, and his father did not have it. What came to him was the knowledge of monotheism, and his father did not have it. ﴿So follow me﴾: the son says to his father, "Follow me," because the son has the truth and the father does not.
﴿I will guide you to a straight path﴾ [Maryam 43]. ﴿O my father, do not worship Satan. Indeed, Satan has been, to the Most Merciful, disobedient﴾ [Maryam 44]. ﴿Do not worship Satan﴾ means the worship of obedience. Whoever obeys something has worshipped it, according to the circumstances. ﴿Indeed, Satan has been disobedient﴾ means "disobedient." ﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would become a companion to Satan﴾ [Maryam 45]: that is, it will befall you. He made being a companion of Satan a form of punishment, because a person turning away from the truth is itself a calamity resulting from some sins, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And if they turn away, then know that Allah only wants to afflict them for some of their sins﴾ [al-Ma'idah 49]. Stop here. We tend to think that punishments are only the trials that befall a person, such as illness, poverty, loss of loved ones, and similar things. This is true, yes, these are punishments, but there is a greater punishment, which is ... ﴿And if they turn away, then know that Allah only wants to afflict them for some of their sins﴾. This is greater than the punishment of a physical, bodily trial. For this reason he said: ﴿O my father, indeed I fear that a punishment from the Most Merciful will touch you, so you would become a companion to Satan﴾ [Maryam 45]. What was the father's reply? The father's reply was harsh: ﴿He said, "Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?"﴾ [Maryam 46]. Look, he denied him his desire. This is why the scholars of rhetoric (*balaghah*) said that the word which comes right after the interrogative particle *hamzah* (همزة الاستفهام) is the element being denied. He did not say, "O Abraham, do you turn away?" Rather, he began with the denial, in the manner of ... ﴿Do you turn away from my gods, O Abraham?﴾. This is an interrogative of denial and rebuke. ﴿If you do not cease﴾ [Maryam 46], meaning: from your calling me to monotheism. ﴿If you do not cease﴾, what?

* Students: ﴿I will surely stone you﴾ [Maryam 46].
* Shaykh: ﴿I will surely stone you.﴾ It is a threat that the father makes to his son, while the son softens toward him and pleads with him, saying, "O father, O father, O father." Here is the father's reply. This statement, ﴿If you do not cease, I will surely stone you﴾, was also said by others who denied the messengers. Pharaoh said to Moses: ﴿I will surely make you one of the imprisoned﴾ [ash-Shu'ara' 29].
﴿And leave me for a long time﴾ [Maryam 46]: that is, abandon me. ﴿For a long time﴾ means a long period. He means: leave me as I am and do not speak to me.
﴿He said, "Peace be upon you"﴾ [Maryam 47]. This is Abraham's final word. How forbearing he was, peace be upon him. This is why Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing﴾ [at-Tawbah 114]. ﴿He said, "Peace be upon you. I will ask forgiveness for you from my Lord. Indeed, He has always been gracious to me"﴾ [Maryam 47]. He asked forgiveness for him until Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, forbade him.

The point of all this is that Abraham's father was a polytheist, is that not so?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: What is his name?
* Students: Azar.
* Shaykh: Azar, as Allah the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar, "Do you take idols as gods?"﴾ [al-An'am 74]. It is strange that some people, may Allah protect us, have distorted the words of Allah away from what He intended, following their own desires. They say: "Abraham's father was not a polytheist; rather he was upon monotheism. It is impossible for the father of a Prophet to be a polytheist. Azar was his paternal uncle, not his father." La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah (there is no might or power except with Allah). See how desire works! "Whoever speaks about the Quran according to his own opinion, let him take his seat in the Fire"[[Narrated by at-Tirmidhi (2951) from the hadith of 'Abdullah ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both.]]. How can one say, "He was not his father but his uncle," when the Quran says: ﴿When Abraham said to his father Azar﴾? How can one say he was his uncle when he says: ﴿O my father﴾? Is the one who says this not ashamed? Does he not fear Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, by altering the words from their places, based on a corrupt belief that the father of a Messenger cannot be a disbeliever? We say: Glory be to Allah! Consider this: that the father of the Messenger was a disbeliever while his son was a great Prophet is the greatest evidence of Allah's power, and that He brings the living out of the dead, and that lineage does not elevate its owners. Is that not so, O people?

* Students: Yes.
* Shaykh: By Allah, if we said this to an elderly woman among the elderly Muslims, that Azar was Abraham's paternal uncle and not his father, she would criticise us. Rather, we say: Abraham's father was a disbeliever, and Muhammad's father was a disbeliever, and what harm does it do to the Prophet that his father was a disbeliever? It harms him in no way. Rather, this is the greatest proof of the perfection of Allah's power, that He brings Prophets out from the loins of these disbelievers. But praise be to Allah, no Prophet has ever come from an illicit union, never. As for the matter of disbelief and faith, this does not count as an affront to the honour of the Prophets.

The point of all this is that Abraham, peace be upon him, openly told his father and his people: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾ [az-Zukhruf 26]. ﴿Free﴾: the mufassir (commentator) said "*bari'*" (بريء), and this is a shortcoming on the part of the mufassir, because *bara'* (براء) is a *sifah mushabbahah* (an adjective-like form, a stable quality), while *bari'* (بريء) is an *ism al-fa'il* (active participle). Which is greater? The *sifah mushabbahah* is greater, because it indicates permanence, stability, and continuity. So *bara'* is greater than *bari'*. ﴿Bara'﴾ means the quality of freedom: a permanent, fixed, continuous disassociation from what you are upon. ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who created me﴾ [az-Zukhruf 26–27]. I think it is not possible to complete the verse; time has run out.

* * *

Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan: ﴿And He made it a lasting word among his descendants that they might return. Rather, I gave enjoyment to these and their fathers until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger. But when the truth came to them, they said, "This is magic, and indeed we are disbelievers in it"﴾ [az-Zukhruf 28–30].

* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿And He made it a lasting word among his descendants that they might return.﴾
* Student: The verse before it.
* Shaykh: The one before it? ﴿And when Abraham said﴾?
* Student: The one after it.
* Shaykh: This is ﴿And He made it a lasting word﴾.
* Student: ﴿Except He who created me, for He will guide me﴾.
* Shaykh: Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And when Abraham said to his father and his people, "Indeed, I am free from what you worship"﴾. Here, *idh* (إذ), what is its position in grammatical analysis?
* Student: Object.
* Shaykh: Why?
* Student: (...)
* Shaykh: The estimate is: "Remember when he said." Yes, remember, meaning to these deniers: remember this statement that Abraham, peace be upon him, made, the one they took pride in claiming descent from and following his religion, so that the proof may be established against them. ﴿When he said﴾. ﴿To his father and his people﴾: his father is Azar, and he had debates with him that were discussed earlier. ﴿And his people﴾ are the ones he was sent to. Abraham, peace be upon him, like the other Prophets, was sent specifically to his own people, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I have been given five things that none of the Prophets before me were given," among them: "A Prophet used to be sent only to his own people, but I have been sent to all mankind"[[Agreed upon (Muttafaq 'alayh); al-Bukhari (438) and Muslim (521/3) from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, may Allah be pleased with them both.]].

﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾. This sentence is emphasised, as is well known, by *inna* (إنّ), and *bara'* (براء) is a *sifah mushabbahah*, which is more eloquent than the word *bari'* (بريء), because the *sifah mushabbahah* implies permanence and stability. ﴿From what you worship﴾: that is, from that which you worship. ﴿Except He who created me﴾. What is meant by "you worship" is the idols they carved with their own hands and then worshipped. This is why Abraham, peace be upon him, said to them in one of his debates: ﴿He said, "Do you worship what you carve, when Allah created you and what you make?"﴾ [as-Saffat 95–96]. How can you worship them when they are created? How can you worship them when you are the ones who carve them? As for His saying ﴿Except He who created me﴾: *illa* (إلا) is the particle of exception. But is the exception here disconnected (*munqati'*) or connected (*muttasil*)? The answer: if they worshipped Allah and other than Him, the exception is connected; if they did not worship Allah, the exception is disconnected. A disconnected exception is one where what follows *illa* is not of the same kind as what precedes it. The grammarians illustrated this with their saying: "The people came except a donkey." Is the donkey of the same kind as the people, or of a different kind?

* Student: Of a different kind.
* Shaykh: Of a different kind, so the exception is disconnected. But if it is said: "The people came except Zayd," the exception here is connected, because Zayd is of the same kind as the one excepted from. So here we apply this rule: ﴿Except He who created me﴾. If they worshipped Allah and other than Him, is the exception...?
* Students: Connected.
* Shaykh: Connected. And if they did not worship Allah, the exception is disconnected. As for His saying ﴿Except He who created me﴾, He did not say "Except Allah," in order to establish the proof that none deserves worship except Him. The One who originated you the first time and brought you into existence from nothing is the One who deserves to be worshipped, because He is the Creator of you. Pay attention.

That is to say, if someone asks: "Why did He not say, 'Except Allah'?" The answer: to establish the proof that none should be worshipped except Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This is like His saying: ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you﴾ [al-Baqarah 21]. It is well known that *Rabb* (رب, Lord) means Creator, yet He said ﴿who created you﴾, though this is already known, in order to establish the proof that He alone deserves worship. ﴿Except He who created me﴾: the author said, "who created me."

﴿For He will guide me﴾: He will guide me to His religion. Guidance is of two kinds, as will be explained, if Allah wills, in the statement of benefits. ﴿And He made it﴾: that is, the word of monotheism understood from His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾ [as-Saffat 99]. ﴿He made it﴾: the pronoun refers to the word he spoke. What was the word he spoke? Listen to the words of the mufassir: he said it is His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me﴾. This is an error on the part of the author. The word he spoke is the nearest word, which is: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship (26), except He who created me﴾, and it is the word of monotheism. As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am going to my Lord, He will guide me﴾, it has no connection to this verse. So ﴿He made it﴾: the pronoun refers to what?

* Student: His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free﴾.
* Shaykh: No. ﴿He made it﴾: the pronoun refers to what? To the word he spoke, which is?
* Student: ﴿Indeed, I am free﴾.
* Shaykh: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship (26), except He who created me﴾. The meaning of His saying ﴿He made it﴾ is: He appointed it as the path that those after him would follow. ﴿A lasting word among his descendants﴾: among whose descendants?

* Student: The descendants of Abraham.
* Shaykh: The descendants of Abraham. He said: that is, his offspring. So there will always be among them someone who affirms the oneness of Allah. This is what the author said: that the meaning is that this word will remain among his descendants, and that the whole progeny cannot associate others with Allah, but that some must remain. The correct view is different from this. The correct meaning is: He made this word the only word that those after him would follow, whether they adhered to it or not.

﴿That they might return﴾: that is, the people of Makkah. If it were said that ﴿that they might return﴾ refers to his descendants, that would be a more general meaning than what the author said, since the verses do not mention the people of Makkah but mention "descendants." It is well known that the people of Makkah are of his descendants, and that the Children of Israel are of his descendants. If we say that the pronoun in ﴿that they might return﴾ refers to ﴿his descendants﴾, it becomes more general than what the author said, because the author limited it to a part of the descendants, and this is clearly a deficiency. For this reason, adopt this principle: do not interpret the Quran in a more restricted sense than what it indicates. In other words, if the Quran indicates something general, do not restrict it unless there is evidence; otherwise leave it in its generality. So ﴿And He made it a lasting word among his descendants that they might return﴾ [az-Zukhruf 28]: the pronoun refers to whom?

* Students: His descendants.
* Shaykh: To the descendants: from Quraysh and the Children of Israel. But what is the meaning of ﴿He made it a lasting word﴾? According to the author, may Allah have mercy on him, the mufassir means that this word will remain among the descendants, so monotheism can never be lost from them. The correct view is that He made it a legislated appointment (*ja'lan shar'iyyan*), meaning that He charged his descendants to worship Allah alone, the Mighty and Majestic. Some of them obeyed, and some of them disobeyed.

* In this noble verse there is a great virtue of Abraham, peace be upon him, which is his declaration of freedom from what his people worshipped: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verses 26–28 (part 2 of 2):**

* Among its lessons: pure monotheism (tawhid) in Ibrahim, based on His saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship, except He who created me﴾. This is the meaning of the words "there is no god but Allah" (la ilaha illa Allah). So "Indeed, I am free" corresponds to "there is no god" (la ilaha), and "except He who created me" corresponds to "but Allah" (illa Allah). Answer me!
* Students: "But Allah" (illa Allah).
* Shaykh: It corresponds to "but Allah." So this statement, ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾, has exactly the meaning of "there is no god but Allah." Is that not so?
* Student: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: Among the benefits of this noble verse: a person should support a ruling with evidence (dalil), because that is more eloquent. This is shown when Ibrahim said: ﴿except He who created me﴾.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: strength of hope, meaning Ibrahim's hope in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, based on his saying: ﴿for indeed He will guide me﴾. The "sin" here (in sa-yahdeni) indicates certainty. Guidance (hidayah) is of two kinds. The first kind is guidance by indication (hidayat al-dalala, the guidance of showing the way), which comes from Allah and from the servants of Allah. The second is guidance to the truth through divine enabling (hidayat al-tawfiq), which comes only from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic; no one possesses it. Listen: guidance is of two kinds. The first?
* Students: Guidance by indication.
* Shaykh: Guidance by indication, meaning pointing to the truth. This comes from Allah and from others. The second is guidance of enabling, which comes only from Allah alone; no one possesses it. We ask Allah to guide us and you.

Then, the verses that mention guidance are of three types: some must be understood as guidance of enabling, some must be understood as guidance of indication, and some include both. Take the words of the worshipper in prayer: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ [al-Fatiha 6]. Does it include…?

* Students: Guidance by indication.
* Shaykh: Both: guidance by indication, which is knowledge, and guidance of enabling, which is action. So, O worshipper, do you feel this when you say: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾? Or do you feel that you are only reciting a Qur'an? Tell us honestly.
* Student: The second.
* Shaykh: Usually the second. Not all people, but most people say ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ reading it as a verse to be recited. They do not feel that the meaning is: guide me, teach me, and enable me to act. They do not feel this. But feel this, so that you know what you are saying "amen" to.

An example of guidance by indication alone is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [al-Shura 52]. What kind of guidance is this?

* Students: Indication.
* Shaykh: Indication, meaning you point people to the straight path. An example of guidance of enabling is the saying of Allah, blessed and exalted: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾ [al-Qasas 56]. He says this to the Messenger (ﷺ), meaning: you cannot grant anyone guidance, even if you love them. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) tried, when his uncle Abu Talib was present in his final moments, to make him profess Allah's oneness, but he was unable. He said at the time of death: "O uncle, say: there is no god but Allah, a word by which I can argue for you before Allah."[[Narrated by al-Bukhari (3884) from the hadith of al-Musayyib ibn Hazn, may Allah be pleased with him.]] Two men of Quraysh who were bad companions were with him, and they said to Abu Talib: "Will you turn away from the religion of Abd al-Muttalib?" See, may Allah protect us, the pride! "Will you turn away from the religion of Abd al-Muttalib?" meaning his grandfather, whom Quraysh took pride in. So the last thing he said was: "He is on the religion of Abd al-Muttalib," and he refused to say: "There is no god but Allah."

So what guidance was the Prophet (ﷺ) unable to give in this case?

* Students: Guidance of enabling.
* Shaykh: Guidance of enabling. As for guidance of indication, he said: "Say: there is no god but Allah."

The saying of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿As for Thamud, We guided them, but they preferred blindness over guidance﴾ [Fussilat 17]. Which of the two kinds is this?

* Students: Indication.
* Shaykh: Guidance of indication. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He chose him and guided him to a straight path﴾ [al-Nahl 121].

* Students: It includes both.
* Shaykh: It includes both together.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the complete sincere advice of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to his descendants (aqib), since he made the word of tawhid remain among them. This is like a bequest to his descendants that they should carry out this bequest.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: returning to the truth that the forefathers held, based on His saying: ﴿so that they may return﴾.

Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Nay, I gave good things to these people and their fathers until there came to them the truth and a clear messenger﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 29]. "Bal" (نَعَم، بل: nay/rather) here is for ʾidrāb, a turning away, either of nullification or of transition.

* Student: Transition.

* The Shaykh: A turning away of transition, to show the favour of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, upon the Quraysh. ﴿I gave good things to these people﴾, the polytheists, meaning I let them remain, ﴿and their fathers﴾, and I did not hasten punishment upon them. Rather, He let them remain without punishment despite their polytheism, their disbelief, and their taking of idols such as al-Lāt, al-ʿUzzā, Hubal and Manāt. ﴿Until﴾ (ḥattā) indicates a limit, meaning: until there came to them ﴿the truth﴾ and ﴿a clear messenger﴾. As for ﴿until there came to them the truth﴾, the author says it means (the Qur'an). The correct view is more general: the Qur'an, Islam and the Sunnah. It is more general than what the author said. We follow the principle we mentioned a little earlier, which is what?

* Students: We do not restrict it.

* The Shaykh: We keep the Qur'an on its generality and do not restrict it. So we say: ﴿the truth had come to them﴾, meaning what the Messenger ﷺ brought of the Qur'an, the Sunnah and other legislative matters. (﴿And a clear messenger﴾: one who makes manifest the knowledge of the legal rulings, and he is Muhammad ﷺ.) ﴿A messenger﴾ is indefinite, to indicate that he is known, and also to indicate glorification. His saying (﴿clear﴾ means one who makes the legal rulings manifest) is correct, and the matter is as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said.

* In this noble verse: the proof that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, holds all things in His hand. If He wills, He lets people enjoy and remain; if He wills, He destroys them. This is shown by ﴿Nay, I gave good things to these people﴾, for the granting of enjoyment is attributed to Him alone.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has wisdom in allowing the disbeliever to remain upon the earth; otherwise He would destroy him. But He has wisdom. Among the wisdom is that the truth should come and he believe in it and be made happy in this world and the Hereafter. Among the wisdom in the continuance of disbelievers is that it be a trial for the believers with these disbelievers, through striving against the disbelievers, and the manifestation of Allah's blessing upon the Muslims through Islam.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: what the Prophet ﷺ brought is truth. If it is reports, they are what? Truthful (ṣidq). If they are rulings, they are just (ʿadl). Nothing in what the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, brought is false; all of it is true.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Muhammad, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, is truly the Messenger of Allah.

* Among its benefits: the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, explained everything his Ummah needs, of good that you should do and of evil that you should avoid.

Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, died, and there was not a bird flapping its wings in the sky except that he had reminded us of knowledge about it."[[Narrated by Aḥmad (21361) from Abū Dharr with the wording: "Muhammad ﷺ left us, and there is no bird moving its wings in the sky except that he reminded us of knowledge from it."]]

If you want the proof of this statement, consider: the Islamic Shariah came to establish Tawhid, which is the greatest matter. It came with an explanation of the prayer, zakat, hajj and fasting. It came with the etiquette of eating and drinking, and the etiquette of relieving oneself, of eating and drinking. It came with the etiquette of dress, even the wearing of a garment: the Shariah explained it, that one enters the right sleeve before the left and removes the left before the right. It came with the etiquette of dealing with people with one another. Everything, minor or major, the Shariah came to explain it. Praise be to Allah. But whoever goes astray goes astray, and whoever is guided is guided.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿But when the truth came to them, they said, "This is magic, and we are disbelievers in it."﴾ [al-Zukhruf 30] (We ask Allah for well-being.) When the truth came to them, they said, "This is magic," meaning the Qur'an, because the Qur'an is the most clear and the most eloquent of speech. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, there is magic in eloquence."[^1] For this reason, the Quraysh would come secretly at night to listen to the Prophet's (ﷺ) recitation, which seized their hearts and drew them powerfully to listen to it. Then they said, "This is magic. Muhammad has enchanted us. Muhammad is a magician, a soothsayer, a madman." ﴿They said, "This is magic, and we are disbelievers in it."﴾ (We ask Allah for well-being.) They emphasised that they were disbelievers in it, because, in their claim, it is—

* Students: "Magician."

* The Shaykh: "Magic. And if the Qur'an is magic, then the one who brought it is a magician. For this reason they gave the Prophet (ﷺ) insulting nicknames so that people would be repelled from his call. But, praise be to Allah, whenever they devised evil, Allah brought about good."

* From the benefits of this verse: the great obstinacy of those who denied the Messenger (ﷺ), since they claimed that what he brought was magic, although it is the truth.

* And from the benefits of the verse: the intensity of their obstinacy, since they openly declared that they were disbelievers in it: ﴿They said, "This is magic, and we are disbelievers in it."﴾

[^1]: Narrated by al-Bukhari (5767) from the hadith of Abdullah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both.

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verses 31–32 (part 1 of 2):

And they also said, when the truth came to them: (﴿And they said, "Why not...?"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 31]: "Hallā" (why not / were it not)), ﴿this Qur'an was not sent down to a great man from the two towns﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 31].

"Law-lā" (why not) here means "hallā" (why not). It has examples, such as the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Why did they not bring four witnesses against him?﴾ [An-Nur 13], meaning: why did they not bring four witnesses against him? And His words: ﴿this Qur'an was sent down to a man from the two towns﴾ are another reason for their rejection of the Qur'an. They say: if this Qur'an had been sent down to a great man from the two towns, namely Makkah and al-Ta'if, then we would have accepted it. But it was not sent down to a great man from the two towns, so we will not accept it. Subhan Allah! How great is their obstinacy! Muhammad ﷺ is the greatest man among the Quraysh. If you look at his lineage, the chain of his forefathers, you will find it so, and if you look at his character and his dealings, you will find it so as well. They used to call him "al-Amin" (the trustworthy). But when the truth came, he became a liar, a sorcerer, a madman, a soothsayer.

So now they have resorted to a second excuse, besides that the Qur'an is sorcery. What is it?
* Students: (...).
* Shaykh: The second excuse, they said: if this Qur'an had been sent down to a great man from the people of al-Ta'if or the people of Makkah, we would have accepted it. But it was sent down to Muhammad, who is not great among his people, so we will not accept it.

The commentator says: (﴿a man from the two towns﴾, meaning: from either of them), either Makkah or al-Ta'if, ﴿great﴾, meaning: honoured among his people. Then he named them, saying: (namely al-Walid ibn al-Mughira in Makkah, or 'Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi in al-Ta'if). This explanation requires evidence. If it is historically established that the people of Makkah meant these two men, then there is nothing strange about it. Otherwise the verse remains general, and they gave this false excuse that the Qur'an was not sent down to a great man from the two towns.

Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32]. The interrogative here is for denial, meaning: is it they who distribute the mercy of Allah, giving this one a share and that one a share, or do they say: this one does not deserve it and that one does? ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32]. The author said: (meaning prophethood). This is also something that is taken against the author. How so?
* Student: He restricted it.
* Shaykh: He restricted it to prophethood, whereas we say: prophethood and other things. They do not distribute the mercy of Allah, neither prophethood, nor strength, nor food, nor drink, nor anything else. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32]. This is a sensory proof that cannot be denied. That is, if they are truthful, that they are the ones who distribute the mercy of Allah, then let them consider: ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32], meaning: We have decreed it. This one is rich, that one is poor, this one is moderate, this one is capable, that one is incapable. Is that not so? Does the Quraysh deny this? They do not deny it, because it is a known, tangible, perceptible matter. ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾, so We made some of them rich and some poor. This is an example. Otherwise we would say: We made some of them strong and some weak, some capable and some incapable. ﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32], and so on to the end.

Questions, five minutes.
* Student: Shaykh, the words ﴿I gave them enjoyment﴾ [Al-Furqan 18]: the doer is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And is Allah described by this?
* Shaykh: The acts of Allah have no limit. The One who gave them enjoyment is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Everything in the universe is by the act of Allah, so there is no limit to them.
* Student: May Allah bless you, Shaykh. Is it permissible for a person to supplicate, saying: "O Lord, guide me with the guidance of success," specifying a particular guidance?
* Shaykh: No. He says: "O Allah, guide me," and intends both kinds of guidance, or he says: "O Allah, teach me and enable me to do righteous deeds."
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, we mentioned that a person should not interpret a verse in a more restricted sense than its wording.
* Shaykh: More restricted than its generality, unless there is evidence.
* Student: Not without evidence, Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. If someone says: this verse ﴿the mercy of your Lord﴾ is mentioned in a context, ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down...?"﴾... Is it restricted to prophethood, that it should be for one of the two men from the two towns, a great one?
* Shaykh: No. We say: yes, the context is about prophethood, but if the wording is general, then prophethood is included in it. For this reason the usuliyyun (scholars of legal theory) said: the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause.
* Student: Does the context not serve as evidence?
* Shaykh: No, it does not serve as evidence, because if we say that it is general, it does not exclude what the context indicates. But if it excludes what the context indicates, it is known that this is not valid. What do we have here?
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two towns?" (31) Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord? We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world, and We have raised some of them above others in degrees, so that some of them may take others in service. And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate.﴾ (32) ﴿And were it not that mankind would be one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses and stairways by which they ascend, (33) and doors for their houses and couches on which they recline, (34) and ornaments of gold. But all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the life of this world. And the Hereafter with your Lord is for the righteous.﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 31–35].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two towns?"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 31]. Who said this? The disbelievers of the Quraysh. And what is meant by "the two towns"?
* Student: Makkah and al-Ta'if.
* Shaykh: Makkah and al-Ta'if. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said, at the beginning of today's lesson: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32]. The interrogative here is for negation, meaning: they are not the ones who distribute the mercy of Allah, to allocate it however they wish. Rather, it is the bounty of Allah: He gives it to whom He wills. The author said: (﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾: prophethood). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, thus restricted it to prophethood, based on their saying: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two towns?﴾. But the correct view regarding this kind of matter is that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause. On this basis we say: what is meant by the mercy of Allah is more general than prophethood. That is, prophethood, abundance of provision, security, large numbers of children, and similar things. Is it they who distribute these? The answer is negative: no.

Then Allah, the Exalted, presented a proof against them that they cannot escape, saying: ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32]. This is something they cannot deny. We made some of them rich and some of them poor.
(﴿And We raised some of them﴾ by wealth), ﴿above others in degrees﴾. He says: (by wealth). But this is also a deficiency. The correct view is that He raised some of them above others in degrees of wealth, knowledge, intellect, character, and other things. Allah raised some people above others in degrees, that is, wide degrees.

﴿so that some of them may take others in service﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32]. The author said: (﴿so that some of them may take﴾: the rich; ﴿others﴾: the poor; ﴿in service﴾: made to work for him for wages; the "ya" is for attribution; and it is read with a kasra on the sin). Allah raised some of them above others in degrees, ﴿so that some of them may take others﴾. The author says: the wealthy, ﴿others﴾: the poor. What do you say?
* Student: Restriction.
* Shaykh: Is this deficient or not?
* Student: Deficient.
* Shaykh: Deficient, because what is meant by ﴿so that some of them may take others in service﴾ is even outside wealth: even in intelligence, even in crafts. For example, a man who has expertise in a craft brings workers, and he is above them. Likewise with intelligence: he sits with people and speaks to them with his exceptional intelligence while they are below that level, and Allah raises him.

The main point is that it is not permissible for us to restrict the Qur'an, to restrict its generality, except with evidence. As for his words, may Allah have mercy on him, (the "ya" is for attribution), meaning the attribution of subjection. As for his words, (it is read with a kasra on the sin), the word "qui'a" (was read) has a technical usage that we must understand. When he says (and in a reading), it is one of the seven readings. When he says (qari'a), it is irregular (shadh), outside the seven readings. Pay attention. The correct view here is that it is an irregular reading, because the sin with a kasra means mockery, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Did We take them in mockery, or have their eyes swerved away from them?﴾ [Sad 63], and He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿So you took them in mockery﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 110], meaning: ridicule. As for the sin with a damma, ﴿sukhriyyan﴾, it is from "taskhir" (subjugation), meaning: to make submissive. Have you understood?

So here are two words, "sikhriyyan" and "sukhriyyan". What is the difference between them?
* Student: "Sikhriyyan" with a kasra is from taskhir.
* Shaykh: "Sikhriyyan" with a kasra is from taskhir. And with a damma?
* Student: "Sukhriyyan" is from sukhriyya (mockery).
* Shaykh: From sukhriyya, you are wrong.
* Student: If it says "sukhriyyan," it is from taskhir.
* Shaykh: "Sukhriyyan" with a damma on the sin is from taskhir.
* Student: And with a kasra, it is from mockery.
* Shaykh: From what?
* Student: From mockery.
* Another student: The reverse, Shaykh.
* Shaykh: There is no power nor strength except with Allah.
* Student: "Sukhriyyan" means subjugation.
* Shaykh: Yes. "Sukhriyyan" with a damma on the sin is from?
* Student: From taskhir.
* Shaykh: From taskhir, which is subjugation.
* Student: And with a kasra, from mockery.
* Shaykh: From "sukhriyya," which is mockery.

Which is appropriate here, the damma or the kasra, in the Qur'an?
* Students: The damma.
* Shaykh: The damma, because it is from taskhir. Were it not for this variation among people, livelihoods would be disrupted. If they were all wealthy, who would do the work? Answer me, everyone.
* Students: No one.
* Shaykh: No one would do it, because if he is asked to work, he says: "If you have a thousand riyals, I have two thousand." The same applies to the other attributes. Were it not for this variation, the world would never have been set in order. This is part of the wisdom of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

Then there is another wisdom: that through this the power of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, becomes known, in that He made humankind of one kind, with one set of powers, and yet they differ greatly in what Allah the Mighty and Majestic has given them of wealth and other things. This is a parenthetical statement (...).
... the Mighty and Majestic: (﴿And the mercy of your Lord﴾, meaning: Paradise; ﴿is better than what they accumulate﴾, meaning: in this world).

As for His words, ﴿And the mercy of your Lord﴾, meaning: Paradise. There is also some deficiency in this. "Mercy" is undoubtedly applied to Paradise, as Allah said to it, addressing it: "You are My mercy; I show mercy through you to whomever I will" [agreed upon; al-Bukhari (4850) and Muslim (2846/34), from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him]. And Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿As for those whose faces turn black, "Did you disbelieve after your belief? Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve." (106) But as for those whose faces turn white, they will be in the mercy of Allah, wherein they will abide eternally﴾ [Al Imran 106–107], meaning: Paradise. But it should be said that the mercy of Allah is more general than this. Even Allah's mercy to the servant in guiding him to Islam and faith is better than what they accumulate. So generalization is better than restriction.

* In this verse there are benefits. Among them: the argument against polytheists with falsehood, by His words. What is the evidence?
* Student: Yes.
* Shaykh: Arguing with the polytheists with falsehood. From where is it derived? Do you not have knowledge?
* Student: His words: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾.
* Shaykh: Wrong.
* Student: His words: ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two towns?"﴾.
* Shaykh: From their saying: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two towns?﴾. The reason is that the Quraysh knew that Muhammad, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, was the most deserving of people of prophethood, had they believed in it, because he was of the best Arab lineage, and because he was the trustworthy and truthful one. They called him "al-Amin" before he came with prophethood.
* Among the benefits of this verse: the word "qarya" (town) is applied to large cities, indeed to the mother of cities, by His words: ﴿from the two towns, a great one﴾, and by His words in another verse: ﴿And how many a town was stronger in might than your town which expelled you﴾ [Muhammad 13]. Which is the town that expelled him?
* Student: Makkah.
* Shaykh: Makkah. In our custom today, "qarya" is applied to a small town. If you said to the people of a large city, "You are the people of a qarya," they would become furious. But it is said: the Qur'an is between us. "Qarya" is applied even to a large city, because it derives from "qary," which means gathering.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: Allah's refutation of them, and clarifying that they are not the ones who distribute the mercy of Allah, by His words: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾.
* Among its benefits: establishing the proof that cannot be disentangled from, that they cannot distribute the mercy of Allah. Is it derived?
* Student: His words: "Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?"
* Shaykh: Wrong.
* Student: His words, the Exalted: ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood﴾.
* Shaykh: It is derived from His words: ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood﴾. They cannot deny this. They know that among them are rich and poor, strong and weak, intelligent and dull, wise and foolish. They know this.
* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the wisdom in Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, making people of different degrees, by His words: ﴿so that some of them may take others in service﴾.
* Among the benefits of the verse: establishing causation and wisdom in the acts of Allah, the Exalted. That is, He, the Mighty and Majestic, acts for a wisdom; it must be for a wisdom, by His words: ﴿so that some of them may take others in service﴾, because the "lam" here indicates causation. The causation of Allah's cosmic decrees is abundant in the Qur'an. Are the legal rulings, such as obligation, prohibition, and permissibility, causally explained?
The answer: yes, they are causally explained. Every ruling of Allah, cosmic or legislative, must have a wisdom. But here is a question: are these wisdoms known to creation, or are they not known?
The answer: some of them are known, and some of them are not known. Is that not so?
* Students: Yes indeed.
* Shaykh: Because our intellects are deficient. However much intellect we reach, it is deficient.
So take this benefit: all the cosmic and legislative rulings of Allah are causally explained by a wisdom. But some of the wisdoms we know, and some we do not know. This is how it must be.
If someone says: which is more eloquent in worship, that one worships Allah without knowing the wisdom, or that one worships Allah knowing the wisdom?
The answer: as for complete humility, a person's worship of something whose wisdom he does not know is more eloquent than his worship of something whose wisdom he knows, because if he worships Allah with something whose wisdom he knows, he may be worshipping Allah for the sake of that wisdom. But if he does not know the wisdom, it becomes more eloquent in humility, as if he is saying: "I will worship Allah whether I know the wisdom of this or not."
An example of this is throwing the pebbles at the Jamarat during Hajj. A person brings specific pebbles and throws them at a specific place. Whereas if he brought many times these pebbles after ten days and threw them at this place, it would be considered pointless. So what is the wisdom?

Answer: The wisdom behind that is to establish the remembrance of Allah; for this reason, whenever a person throws, he says, "Allahu akbar." Second: it manifests the effect of pure devotion (ta'abbud mutlaq), whereby a person performs this action without knowing its precise purpose, and similar matters are many.

For this reason, the jurists (fuqaha'), may Allah have mercy on them, applied the term ta'abbudiyyah (acts of pure devotion) to rulings whose wisdom is not known, or said "this is ta'abbud" or the like, because its purpose is nothing other than establishing worship of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the permissibility of employing workers, from His words: ﴿that some of them may take others in service⁠﴾.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: the great wisdom in this, namely in the disparity (among people), for were it not for this disparity, the value of Allah's blessing would not be recognized in the wealthy with wealth, in the intelligent with intellect, in the strong with strength, and so on. Is that not so?

* Students: Yes indeed.

* The Shaykh: Yes. Were it not for madness, the value of intellect would not be recognized; were it not for sickness, the value of health would not be recognized. Do you agree with this?

* Students: Yes.

* The Shaykh: So then, this is part of the wisdom.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: that the mercy of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, which includes Paradise, is better than what they amass, that is, better than everything they gather; for Allah is the goal that every believer strives for, indeed every sensible person must strive for it.

* Among the benefits of this noble verse: an indication of the danger of accumulation, that is, the accumulation of wealth, and that this may cause one to forget the Hereafter. And so it is: the accumulation of wealth causes one to forget the Hereafter, except for those whom my Lord has mercy upon. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "By Allah, it is not poverty that I fear for you, but I fear that the world will be opened up to you, and you will compete for it as those before you competed for it, and it will destroy you as it destroyed them."[[Agreed upon; al-Bukhari (3158) and Muslim (2961/6) from the hadith of 'Amr ibn 'Awf al-Ansari, may Allah be pleased with him, and its wording: "...So rejoice and hope for what pleases you, for by Allah, it is not poverty that I fear for you, but I fear that the world will be spread out for you as it was spread out for those before you, and you will compete for it as they competed for it, and it will destroy you as it destroyed them." The hadith.]] This is the reality: worldly life and religion generally do not coexist, except for those whom Allah has mercy upon. How many a person was poor yet upright upon the religion of Allah, then Allah made him rich, and his riches became the cause of his transgression and his independence from his Lord. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Nay! Indeed, man transgresses, when he sees himself self-sufficient⁠﴾ [Al-'Alaq 6–7].

Commentary of Ibn 'Uthaymin (Tafsir al-Quran al-Karim) on surah 43, verses 31–32 (part 1 of 2):

And they also said, when the truth came to them: (﴿And they said, "Why not...?"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 31]: "Hallā" (why not / were it not)), ﴿this Qur'an was not sent down to a great man from the two towns﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 31].

The author said: (meaning prophethood). This is also something that is taken against the author. How so?

* Shaykh: He restricted it to prophethood, whereas we say: prophethood and other things. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32]. This is a sensory proof that cannot be denied. That is, if they are truthful, that they are the ones who distribute the mercy of Allah, then let them consider: ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32], meaning: We have decreed it. This one is rich, that one is poor, this one is moderate, this one is capable, that one is incapable. Is that not so? Does the Quraysh deny this? They do not deny it, because it is a known, tangible, perceptible matter. ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾, so We made some of them rich and some poor. This is an example. Otherwise we would say: We made some of them strong and some weak, some capable and some incapable. ﴿And We raised some of them above others in degrees﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32], and so on to the end.

Questions, five minutes.
* Student: Shaykh, the words ﴿I gave them enjoyment﴾ [Al-Furqan 18]: the doer is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic?
* Shaykh: Yes.
* Student: And is Allah described by this?
* Shaykh: The acts of Allah have no limit. The One who gave them enjoyment is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. Everything in the universe is by the act of Allah, so there is no limit to them.
* Student: May Allah bless you, Shaykh. Is it permissible for a person to supplicate, saying: "O Lord, guide me with the guidance of success," specifying a particular guidance?
* Shaykh: No. He says: "O Allah, guide me," and intends both kinds of guidance, or he says: "O Allah, teach me and enable me to do righteous deeds."
* Student: Shaykh, may Allah be good to you, we mentioned that a person should not interpret a verse in a more restricted sense than its wording.
* Shaykh: More restricted than its generality, unless there is evidence.
* Student: Not without evidence, Shaykh, may Allah be good to you. If someone says: this verse ﴿the mercy of your Lord﴾ is mentioned in a context, ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down...?"﴾... Is it restricted to prophethood, that it should be for one of the two men from the two towns, a great one?
* Shaykh: No. We say: yes, the context is about prophethood, but if the wording is general, then prophethood is included in it. For this reason the usuliyyun (scholars of legal theory) said: the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause.
* Student: Does the context not serve as evidence?
* Shaykh: No, it does not serve as evidence, because if we say that it is general, it does not exclude what the context indicates. But if it excludes what the context indicates, it is known that this is not valid. What do we have here?
* * *
* Student: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two towns?" (31) Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord? We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world, and We have raised some of them above others in degrees, so that some of them may take others in service. And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate.﴾ (32) ﴿And were it not that mankind would be one community, We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses and stairways by which they ascend, (33) and doors for their houses and couches on which they recline, (34) and ornaments of gold. But all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the life of this world. And the Hereafter with your Lord is for the righteous.﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 31–35].
* Shaykh: I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, said: ﴿And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two towns?"﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 31]. Who said this? The disbelievers of the Quraysh. And what is meant by "the two towns"?
* Student: Makkah and al-Ta'if.
* Shaykh: Makkah and al-Ta'if. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said, at the beginning of today's lesson: ﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32]. The interrogative here is for negation, meaning: they are not the ones who distribute the mercy of Allah, to allocate it however they wish. Rather, it is the bounty of Allah: He gives it to whom He wills. The author said: (﴿Is it they who distribute the mercy of your Lord?﴾: prophethood). The author, may Allah have mercy on him, thus restricted it to prophethood, based on their saying: ﴿Why was this Qur'an not sent down to a great man from the two towns?﴾. But the correct view regarding this kind of matter is that the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause. On this basis we say: what is meant by the mercy of Allah is more general than prophethood. That is, prophethood, abundance of provision, security, large numbers of children, and similar things. Is it they who distribute these? The answer is negative: no.

Then Allah, the Exalted, presented a proof against them that they cannot escape, saying: ﴿We have distributed among them their livelihood in the life of this world﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32]. This is something they cannot deny. We made some of them rich and some of them poor.
(﴿And We raised some of them﴾ by wealth), ﴿above others in degrees﴾. He says: (by wealth). But this is also a deficiency. The correct view is that He raised some of them above others in degrees of wealth, knowledge, intellect, character, and other things. Allah raised some people above others in degrees, that is, wide degrees.

﴿so that some of them may take others in service﴾ [Az-Zukhruf 32]. The author said: (﴿so that some of them may take﴾: the rich; ﴿others﴾: the poor; ﴿in service﴾: made to work for him for wages; the "ya" is for attribution; and it is read with a kasra on the sin). Allah raised some of them above others in degrees, ﴿so that some of them may take others﴾. The author says: the wealthy, ﴿others﴾: the poor. What do you say?
* Student: Restriction.
* Shaykh: Is this deficient or not?
* Student: Deficient.
* Shaykh: Deficient, because what is meant by ﴿so that some of them may take others in service﴾ is even outside wealth: even in intelligence, even in crafts. For example, a man who has expertise in a craft brings workers, and he is above them. Likewise with intelligence: he sits with people and speaks to them with his exceptional intelligence while they are below that level, and Allah raises him.

The main point is that it is not permissible for us to restrict the Qur'an, to restrict its generality, except with evidence. As for his words, may Allah have mercy on him, (the "ya" is for attribution), meaning the attribution of subjection. As for his words, (it is read with a kasra on the sin), the word "qui'a" (was read) has a technical usage that we must understand. When he says (and in a reading), it is one of the seven readings. When he says (qari'a), it is irregular (shadh), outside the seven readings. Pay attention. The correct view here is that it is an irregular reading, because the sin with a kasra means mockery, as Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿Did We take them in mockery, or have their eyes swerved away from them?﴾ [Sad 63], and He, glorified and exalted, said: ﴿So you took them in mockery﴾ [Al-Mu'minun 110], meaning: ridicule. As for the sin with a damma, ﴿sukhriyyan﴾, it is from "taskhir" (subjugation), meaning: to make submissive. Have you understood?

So here are two words, "sikhriyyan" and "sukhriyyan". What is the difference between them?
* Student: "Sikhriyyan" with a kasra is from taskhir.
* Shaykh: "Sikhriyyan" with a kasra is from taskhir. And with a damma?
* Student: "Sukhriyyan" is from sukhriyya (mockery).
* Shaykh: From sukhriyya, you are wrong.
* Student: If it says "sukhriyyan," it is from taskhir.
* Shaykh: "Sukhriyyan" with a damma on the sin is from taskhir.
